Ishmaiah of Gibeon, who is marked out as a mighty man among the thirty and a leader over the thirty. Jozabad of Gederah, Shephatiah the Haruphite, the Korahites, the sons of Jeroham of Gedor.

Roughly two dozen men, and about half of them are pinned to a village. That is the point of a list like this to the people first reading it. These are not legends; they are somebody's great-grandfather from a place you can walk to in an afternoon.

The community the Chronicler wrote for was a few thousand returned exiles rebuilding a provincial town, and their besetting fear was that they were too small to matter. He hands them a list of men from Gibeah and Gibeon and Gederah who changed the history of Israel by getting up and walking to Ziklag, and he does not tell them what to make of it.

verseByVerse.quote: From the Gadites there went over to David at the stronghold in the wilderness mighty and experienced warriors, expert with shield and spear, whose faces were like the faces of lions and who were swift as gazelles upon the mountains: Ezer the chief, Obadiah second, Eliab third, Mishmannah fourth, Jeremiah fifth, Attai sixth, Eliel seventh, Johanan eighth, Elzabad ninth, Jeremiah tenth, Machbannai eleventh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Gadites lived east of the Jordan, on the far side of the river from everything the story cares about, and chapter 5 had reported the end of that story before this chapter began: the trans-Jordan tribes broke faith with the God of their fathers and were carried into exile. Here, generations earlier, their fighting men are crossing the water in the opposite direction to find a fugitive in a desert hole.

Then a sentence of portraiture, which no muster roll needs. Mighty and experienced warriors, expert with shield and spear, whose faces were like the faces of lions and who were swift as gazelles upon the mountains. A lion's face is what an enemy sees; a gazelle's speed is what he cannot catch. Somebody who had fought alongside these men remembered them well enough to say both at once.

Then eleven names with a number attached to each: Ezer the chief, Obadiah second, Eliab third, down to Machbannai eleventh. They were ranked, and the ranking was written down, and the man who came eleventh is in Scripture by name.

It is a small thing and it says something about how God keeps records. There is a public and permanent register of an eleventh-best swordsman from a tribe that would later be deported for unfaithfulness, and he is in it because for one season of his life he risked everything on the LORD's anointed. Nothing done for the true King is filed under also-ran.

verseByVerse.quote: These Gadites were officers of the army; the least was a match for a hundred men and the greatest for a thousand. These are the men who crossed the Jordan in the first month, when it was overflowing all its banks, and put to flight all those in the valleys, to the east and to the west.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two verses of assessment, and both of them are measurements.

The first: the least was a match for a hundred men and the greatest for a thousand. Even allowing for the way soldiers talk about soldiers, the sentence is telling us that David's desert band had gone from four hundred debtors and malcontents to a corps of professionals, and that the change happened while nothing outwardly was going his way at all.

The second measurement is the river. These are the men who crossed the Jordan in the first month, when it was overflowing all its banks.

The first month is Nisan, spring, when the snow comes off Hermon and the Jordan runs high and wide and fast. It is the one season nobody crosses. It is also the exact month and the exact condition of the river when Joshua brought Israel over into the land, and the reader who has been given chapters of genealogy running back to Adam will hear the echo. But there is no ark here, and no dry ground, and no priests standing in the riverbed. These men went into the flood and swam.

And having crossed it they scattered everyone in the valleys east and west, which means they came out of the water fighting on both banks. The Chronicler has no comment to add. He sets down what the water was doing and what they did anyway, and lets the two facts sit next to each other.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Men of Benjamin and Judah arrive together, and David — who has been sold twice already by his own countrymen — meets them at the gate and says it plainly: if you have come to help me my heart will be joined to yours, and if to betray me, may the God of our fathers see and rebuke you (v. 17). He has no way to test them. Then the Spirit clothed Amasai, and out comes an oath in verse: We are yours, O David ... For your God helps you (v. 18). David takes them in. A parenthesis admits the ugliest fact of the outlaw years — David marched out with the Philistines against Saul, and was sent home by suspicious pagans (vv. 19-20). The section ends with the trickle become a flood: from day to day men came to David to help him, until there was a great army, like an army of God (v. 22).
verseByVerse.theology: Seven times in this stretch of the chapter somebody helps somebody, and in the middle of the run the Spirit takes the word away from the men and gives it to God: your God helps you. The army is real, and the army is not the reason David will reign.
verseByVerse.examples: David could not tell friend from assassin by looking, so he put the question in front of God and waited. That is what a man does when discernment runs out and a decision still has to be made.

verseByVerse.quote: And some of the men of Benjamin and Judah came to the stronghold to David. David went out to meet them and said to them, "If you have come to me in friendship to help me, my heart will be joined to you; but if to betray me to my adversaries, although there is no wrong in my hands, then may the God of our fathers see and rebuke you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A mixed party now — some of the men of Benjamin and Judah, which is a strange combination, because Benjamin is Saul's tribe and Judah is David's, and men from both arrive at the stronghold together.

David goes out to meet them himself, and what he says is one of the most exposed things he ever said. If you have come to me in friendship to help me, my heart will be joined to you; but if to betray me to my adversaries, although there is no wrong in my hands, then may the God of our fathers see and rebuke you.

He has grounds. The men of Keilah, whose town he had just saved from a Philistine raid, were ready to hand him over. The Ziphites went up to Saul twice and volunteered his hiding places. Doeg had watched him take bread from a priest and reported it, and eighty-five priests were killed for the report. David has learned that a man can smile at you in the morning and sell you before dark.

So he does two things at once. He tells them exactly what he is afraid of, out loud, before he has any evidence either way. And having no way on earth to see inside them, he hands the question to the one who can: may the God of our fathers see and rebuke you.

There is a way of living with people that this describes. He does not pretend the suspicion is not there and he does not act on it. He names it, refuses to let it harden into a policy, and puts the judgment where the judgment belongs. Then he waits to see what God will do with the men standing in front of him — which turns out to be the next verse.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the Spirit clothed Amasai, chief of the thirty, and he said, "We are yours, O David, and with you, O son of Jesse! Peace, peace to you, and peace to your helpers! For your God helps you." Then David received them and made them officers of his troops.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David has asked a question he has no means of answering, and the answer arrives from outside the exchange altogether. Then the Spirit clothed Amasai, chief of the thirty.

The verb is the ordinary word for putting on a garment. The Spirit did not fall on Amasai or rest upon him; the Spirit clothed himself with the man and wore him. It is what happened to Gideon before he put the trumpet to his lips, and to Zechariah the priest before he stood in the temple court and said the thing that got him stoned. A man becomes the clothing God speaks through, and what comes out is not the man's own.

And what comes out here is poetry. We are yours, O David, and with you, O son of Jesse! Peace, peace to you, and peace to your helpers! For your God helps you.

Take the title first, because it is doing the hardest work in the sentence. Son of Jesse was an insult. Saul used it at his own table when he could not bring himself to say the name. Nabal used it when he refused the man food. A generation later a rebel would raise the northern tribes on it, shouting that Israel had no inheritance in the son of Jesse. Everyone who ever wanted to cut David down to size reached for that phrase, meaning: a smallholder's boy from a village nobody visits.

Amasai picks the sneer up and swears by it. He is not pledging himself to a royal personage; he is pledging himself, deliberately and by name, to the son of Jesse of Bethlehem, and he does it while that man is a fugitive with nothing to offer. The insult becomes the oath. Something like that happens again when a title fixed to a cross as a charge — king of the Jews — turns out to be the plain truth, and the church has been swearing by it ever since.

Then peace, three times over, spreading outward: to you, and to your helpers, and to you again. And the last clause takes the whole speech and moves it off David. For your God helps you. Amasai has just handed over an army and in the same breath told the king that the army is not the reason he will win.

Nobody had asked for any of this. David asked about motives; the Spirit answered with a confession of faith, and the man who made it had no idea an hour earlier that he was going to. Then David received them and made them officers of his troops — the suspicion is over, and it was ended by God speaking through the very men who were under suspicion. The LORD has never yet left his anointed standing at a gate without a witness.

verseByVerse.quote: Some of the men of Manasseh deserted to David when he came with the Philistines for the battle against Saul. (Yet he did not help them, for the rulers of the Philistines took counsel and sent him away, saying, "At peril to our heads he will desert to his master Saul.") As he went to Ziklag, these men of Manasseh deserted to him: Adnah, Jozabad, Jediael, Michael, Jozabad, Elihu, and Zillethai, chiefs of thousands in Manasseh. They helped David against the band of raiders, for they were all mighty men of valor and were commanders in the army.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now a sentence the Chronicler could have left out, and did not.

Some of the men of Manasseh deserted to David when he came with the Philistines for the battle against Saul.

Read it slowly. On the day Israel was destroyed at Gilboa and Saul and Jonathan died, David was marching in the Philistine order of battle. He was not a spectator; he had brought his men, and he was in the line with the enemies of God's people against God's people. The outlaw years had taken him that far.

What kept him out of it is in the brackets. Yet he did not help them, for the rulers of the Philistines took counsel and sent him away, saying, At peril to our heads he will desert to his master Saul. Five pagan warlords held a meeting, decided the Hebrew could not be trusted, and sent him home. They were protecting their own necks. They were also, without the faintest idea of it, keeping the future king of Israel from having Israelite blood on his hands on the day the throne fell vacant.

David did not extract himself from that position; he was extracted, by men who despised him, for reasons that had nothing to do with him. It is not a comfortable kind of rescue and it is the kind that most often arrives. The mess had been walked into with open eyes, and God got him out of it through the suspicion of the very people he had been leaning on.

Seven officers of Manasseh came over during that retreat, and the text says what they were immediately good for: they helped David against the band of raiders. That is the Amalekite raid that burned Ziklag to the ground and carried off every wife and child in it while the men were away. They arrived, it turned out, four days before the worst day of David's life. He did not know that when he took them in.

verseByVerse.quote: For from day to day men came to David to help him, until there was a great army, like an army of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For from day to day men came to David to help him, until there was a great army, like an army of God.

Day to day. Not a movement, not a rising, not a moment when the country turned. Two men this week and a dozen the next, walking in from Gibeah and Gilead and the far side of the river, one decision at a time, over years, until somebody counted and found there was an army.

That is how it was built, and the Chronicler has spent twenty-one verses proving it by naming them. Nobody in the chapter arrives as part of a crowd. Each of them made a private calculation about a hunted man and a promise, and got up.

Then the phrase at the end: like an army of God. It is the word Jacob used when the angels of God met him on the road home and he called the place Mahanaim, God's camp. The Chronicler is not saying David's men were angels. He is saying that if you had stood on a ridge and watched this force assemble out of nothing around a man with no crown and no capital and no army pay, the only thing you would have had to compare it to was a host that does not come from earth at all.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Now the roll of what came to Hebron to turn the kingdom of Saul over to him, according to the word of the LORD (v. 23). Twelve tribes, counted: Judah 6,800 and Simeon 7,100; the Levites 4,600, with Jehoiada of Aaron's house and a young man named Zadok (vv. 26-28); Benjamin only 3,000, of whom the majority had to that point kept their allegiance to the house of Saul (v. 29); Ephraim and half-Manasseh in their thousands; two hundred chiefs of Issachar who had understanding of the times, to know what Israel ought to do (v. 32); Zebulun's fifty thousand who came with singleness of purpose (v. 33); and at the end the largest contingent of all, 120,000 from beyond the Jordan (v. 37).
verseByVerse.theology: The muster is headed by a clause that governs it: this happened according to the word of the LORD. Three hundred and forty thousand men made a decision, and the Chronicler files the whole of it under a promise God had made to a shepherd boy years before anyone counted anything.
verseByVerse.examples: Two hundred men of Issachar are listed among hundreds of thousands of soldiers, and what they contributed was judgment. A community that counts only what it can arm itself with will not notice when it has lost the people who can tell it what time it is.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the numbers of the divisions of the armed troops who came to David in Hebron to turn the kingdom of Saul over to him, according to the word of the LORD. The men of Judah bearing shield and spear were 6,800 armed troops. Of the Simeonites, mighty men of valor for war, 7,100. Of the Levites 4,600. The prince Jehoiada, of the house of Aaron, and with him 3,700. Zadok, a young man mighty in valor, and twenty-two commanders from his own fathers' house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The scene moves to Hebron, and the register changes from names to numbers. These are the numbers of the divisions of the armed troops who came to David in Hebron to turn the kingdom of Saul over to him, according to the word of the LORD.

That last clause governs everything counted after it. Three hundred and forty thousand men are about to be tallied by tribe, and before a single figure is given the Chronicler files the whole transaction under a promise. This is not a coup and it is not an election result. It is a word God spoke about a shepherd boy catching up with the arithmetic.

Judah first, and the number is small: 6,800. David's own tribe, and it sends fewer men than Simeon. There is a reason — Judah had already crowned him seven years earlier and had been fighting for him ever since. A tribe that has been committed the longest has the least left to prove at the parade.

Then the Levites, 4,600, with Jehoiada the prince of Aaron's house and 3,700 with him. The priests came armed. The men whose work was the altar turned out for the muster like everybody else, and the Chronicler, who cares more about Levites than any other writer in the Old Testament, counts them among the troops without a word of apology.

And in verse 28, in a list of thousands, a young man with twenty-two officers behind him: Zadok, a young man mighty in valor. It is the first time this book has said his name. He will stand by David when Absalom drives him out, he will anoint Solomon at Gihon while another man is being proclaimed on the other side of the ridge, and his descendants will hold the sanctuary so long that Ezekiel, in exile, still measures a faithful priesthood by the sons of Zadok. He enters Scripture here, unannounced, as a youngster with a sword who guessed right about the king.

verseByVerse.quote: Of the Benjaminites, the kinsmen of Saul, 3,000, of whom the majority had to that point kept their allegiance to the house of Saul. Of the Ephraimites 20,800, mighty men of valor, famous men in their fathers' houses. Of the half-tribe of Manasseh 18,000, who were expressly named to come and make David king.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Benjamin: 3,000 — and then a clause no propagandist would have written. Of whom the majority had to that point kept their allegiance to the house of Saul.

Most of Saul's tribe had not come. They were not at Hebron out of conviction; they came late, and the record says so. This is the same book that has just spent seven verses honouring Benjaminites who defected to Ziklag when it was dangerous, and it will not let the exception stand in for the tribe. Some of Benjamin were heroes and most of Benjamin held on to a dead king's household as long as it was standing.

The Chronicler keeps doing this. He is writing to persuade a discouraged community that God's purposes go forward, and he could have smoothed the sentence into nothing. Instead he reports a divided tribe arriving with mixed motives at a coronation that God had already decided, and the coronation happens anyway.

Ephraim sends 20,800, famous men in their fathers' houses, and half-Manasseh 18,000 who were expressly named to come and make David king. Somebody in Manasseh sat down and wrote out a list of who was going. The commitment was not a mood on the day; it was minuted in advance, name by name, by men who intended to be held to it.

verseByVerse.quote: Of Issachar, men who had understanding of the times, to know what Israel ought to do, 200 chiefs, and all their kinsmen under their command.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Of Issachar, men who had understanding of the times, to know what Israel ought to do, 200 chiefs, and all their kinsmen under their command.

Two hundred. In a chapter where Zebulun sends fifty thousand and the eastern tribes send a hundred and twenty thousand, Issachar is entered on the roll with two hundred men, and the reason they are counted at all is that they could tell what time it was.

Notice the two halves of the description, because the second is where the weight falls. Understanding the times is diagnosis: seeing what is actually happening rather than what the last ten years have trained you to expect. Knowing what Israel ought to do is the harder half, and plenty of people manage the first without ever getting to it. The verse does not commend men who had opinions about the moment. It commends men who could say, concretely, what the next step was, and whose relatives were prepared to move when they said it.

And what was it they discerned? Not a trend and not a mood. Verse 23 has already said it: the kingdom was turning over to David according to the word of the LORD. That is the time they understood. They had heard what God had said and they could see it arriving, and reading the moment meant lining their tribe up with a promise while the outcome was still open.

Which sets a test. Anyone can be knowing about the age they live in; the commentary is cheap and endless. The question this verse puts is whether your reading of the times is governed by what God has actually said, and whether it ends in something to do. Diagnosis that never reaches a next step is not the gift of Issachar. It is talk with a serious face.

verseByVerse.quote: Of Zebulun 50,000 seasoned troops, equipped for battle with all the weapons of war, to help David with singleness of purpose. Of Naphtali 1,000 commanders with whom were 37,000 men armed with shield and spear. Of the Danites 28,600 men equipped for battle. Of Asher 40,000 seasoned troops ready for battle. Of the Reubenites and Gadites and the half-tribe of Manasseh from beyond the Jordan, 120,000 men armed with all the weapons of war.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Zebulun sends 50,000 seasoned troops, equipped for battle with all the weapons of war, to help David with singleness of purpose. Underneath that last phrase the Hebrew says something plainer: not with a double heart. They came without keeping anything back for the other outcome.

That is the second thread running through this chapter, alongside the helping. Heart language keeps surfacing — David offering to have his heart joined to theirs, Zebulun undivided, and in a few verses the whole assembly arriving with a whole heart. A double heart is not treachery. It is a man who marches with you and privately keeps a line open to the other side, and it is the ordinary condition of most allegiance most of the time.

Then Naphtali with a thousand commanders and thirty-seven thousand men behind them, the Danites 28,600, Asher 40,000. Dan and Zebulun are worth a second look: those are the two tribes the long genealogy of chapters 2 to 8 never gave a list to. They are missing from the family record and they are both here, in the field, in strength, making David king. Absence from a register is not absence from the people of God.

And the largest contingent in Israel comes from the place with the least reason to send one: of the Reubenites and Gadites and the half-tribe of Manasseh from beyond the Jordan, 120,000 men armed with all the weapons of war. Those tribes had asked Moses for land outside the promise and got it. They were furthest from Hebron, furthest from the sanctuary, and would be the first taken into exile for breaking faith. And on this day they outnumbered everyone. The reach of the king ran out past the river to the people on the edge of the map, and they came.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 38–40 — Three Days at the Table
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter that began with a fugitive in a Philistine town ends with a feast. The men come with a whole heart, and the rest of Israel is of a single mind (v. 38). They stay three days, eating and drinking what their brothers had prepared (v. 39), and the supply train comes in from the far north — donkeys and camels and mules and oxen loaded with flour, fig cakes, raisins, wine and oil (v. 40). The last four words are the verdict on the whole chapter: there was joy in Israel.
verseByVerse.theology: An army was raised and no battle was fought. The kingdom of God's choosing arrives, in this chapter, as a table with enough on it for everybody and three days set aside to sit at it.
verseByVerse.examples: The food came from Issachar, Zebulun and Naphtali — the tribes with the longest walk. The people who had furthest to come brought the provisions.

verseByVerse.quote: All these, men of war, arrayed in battle order, came to Hebron with a whole heart to make David king over all Israel. Likewise, all the rest of Israel were of a single mind to make David king. And they were there with David for three days, eating and drinking, for their brothers had made preparation for them. And also their relatives, from as far as Issachar and Zebulun and Naphtali, came bringing food on donkeys and on camels and on mules and on oxen, abundant provisions of flour, cakes of figs, clusters of raisins, and wine and oil, oxen and sheep, for there was joy in Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All these, men of war, arrayed in battle order, came to Hebron with a whole heart to make David king over all Israel. Likewise, all the rest of Israel were of a single mind to make David king.

Arrayed in battle order, and there is no battle. Three hundred and forty thousand armed men march to Hebron in formation and the thing they do when they arrive is sit down and eat for three days.

The provisioning is described in the kind of detail that only comes from somebody who was pleased about it. Donkeys, camels, mules and oxen; flour, cakes of figs, clusters of raisins, wine, oil, oxen and sheep. And it came from as far as Issachar and Zebulun and Naphtali — the northern tribes, the longest road. The people with the furthest to travel loaded the food.

Set the two ends of this chapter beside each other. It opens with one man who cannot walk about in his own country and a handful of defectors slipping into a Philistine town. It closes with every tribe in Israel around a table with more than they can eat, and the narrator's summary is four words long: there was joy in Israel.

Nothing in between was engineered by David. He did not recruit the Benjaminites, he could not tell whether the men at the gate meant to kill him, and he was standing in a Philistine column on the day the throne fell empty. The kingdom assembled itself around him, day by day, according to a word God had spoken before any of it started.

And this is the shape the story keeps. A rejected king with a handful of followers who came to him while it cost something; then, at the end, a countless multitude out of every tribe, gathered from the far edges of the map, seated at a table that somebody else provided. The last book of the Bible calls it the marriage supper of the Lamb. Hebron was three days and a rumour of it, and there was joy in Israel.

12.theology:
Seven times in twenty-two verses somebody helps somebody. The men helped him in war (v. 1); David asks whether they have come to help him (v. 17); the Manassites helped David (v. 21); men kept coming to help him (v. 22). And at the centre of the run the Spirit takes the word off the men and puts it where it belongs: peace to your helpers! For your God helps you (v. 18). The help is real and it is not the explanation. This is the same move the book made at 11:9 and 11:14, and it is the Chronicler's settled way of telling a story.

And the whole muster stands under one clause: they came according to the word of the LORD (v. 23). Hundreds of thousands of free decisions — a Benjaminite weighing his family, a Gadite looking at the river, a tribe minuting the names of who would go — and not one of them is treated as less than a decision, and all of them together are treated as the keeping of a promise. Scripture never asks which it was.
12.examples:
Amasai took the insult that had been used to belittle David and made it his oath: We are yours, O David, and with you, O son of Jesse. Confessing Christ works the same way. The name was fixed above his head as a criminal charge, and the church has been swearing allegiance by it ever since.

Two hundred men of Issachar were counted for one thing: they understood the times and knew what Israel ought to do. Both halves are required. Reading the moment is a gift; it becomes the gift of Issachar only when it ends in a next step and somebody actually moves.

Zebulun came with no double heart, and the assembly came with a whole one. Divided loyalty rarely announces itself as betrayal. It looks like marching in the column while quietly keeping a line open to the other outcome, and it is the ordinary condition of most allegiance most of the time.

13.title: The Ark and Uzzah: When Good Intentions Are Not Enough
13.text: <sup>1</sup>David consulted with the commanders of thousands and of hundreds, with every leader.<sup>2</sup>And David said to all the assembly of Israel, "If it seems good to you and from the LORD our God, let us send abroad to our brothers who remain in all the lands of Israel, as well as to the priests and Levites in the cities that have pasturelands, that they may be gathered to us.<sup>3</sup>Then let us bring again the ark of our God to us, for we did not seek it in the days of Saul."<sup>4</sup>All the assembly agreed to do so, for the thing was right in the eyes of all the people.<sup>5</sup>So David assembled all Israel from the Nile of Egypt to Lebo-hamath, to bring the ark of God from Kiriath-jearim.<sup>6</sup>And David and all Israel went up to Baalah, that is, to Kiriath-jearim that belongs to Judah, to bring up from there the ark of God, which is called by the name of the LORD who sits enthroned above the cherubim.<sup>7</sup>And they carried the ark of God on a new cart, from the house of Abinadab, and Uzzah and Ahio were driving the cart.<sup>8</sup>And David and all Israel were celebrating before God with all their might, with song and lyres and harps and tambourines and cymbals and trumpets.<sup>9</sup>And when they came to the threshing floor of Chidon, Uzzah put out his hand to take hold of the ark, for the oxen stumbled.<sup>10</sup>And the anger of the LORD was kindled against Uzzah, and he struck him down because he put out his hand to the ark, and he died there before God.<sup>11</sup>And David was angry because the LORD had broken out against Uzzah. And that place is called Perez-uzza to this day.<sup>12</sup>And David was afraid of God that day, and he said, "How can I bring the ark of God home to me?"<sup>13</sup>So David did not take the ark home into the city of David, but took it aside to the house of Obed-edom the Gittite.<sup>14</sup>And the ark of God remained with the household of Obed-edom in his house three months. And the LORD blessed the household of Obed-edom and all that he had.
13.overview:
David's first act as king of a united Israel is to go and get the ark. He consults the commanders and the assembly (vv. 1-4), summons the nation from the Nile of Egypt to Lebo-hamath (v. 5), and fetches the ark from Kiriath-jearim on a new cart with singing and every instrument Israel owned (vv. 6-8). At the threshing floor of Chidon the oxen stumble, Uzzah steadies the ark and is struck dead (vv. 9-10). David is angry, then afraid, and diverts the ark to the house of Obed-edom, where it stays three months and the household is blessed (vv. 11-14).

The chapter is not a story about a man who made one mistake. It is a story about a nation doing a right thing in a way it had never checked, with the men who were supposed to carry the ark walking beside the cart it was riding on.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — All Israel, and a New Cart
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David's first project as king of the whole nation is to fetch the ark. He consults every commander and puts it to the assembly with two tests in one sentence — if it seems good to you and from the LORD our God (v. 2) — and names the reason it has to be done: we did not seek it in the days of Saul (v. 3). All Israel is summoned from one end of the land to the other (v. 5), and they go up to Kiriath-jearim for the ark which is called by the name of the LORD who sits enthroned above the cherubim (v. 6). Then the detail on which the whole chapter turns: they carried the ark of God on a new cart (v. 7), with the singing and the lyres and the tambourines going before it (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 3 is the hinge of the book. Saul did not seek the LORD and died for it (10:13-14); David's first act is to go and seek him. The Chronicler has been building to this word since the obituary of the last king, and he will keep it running to the last charge David ever gives his son.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 2 summons the priests and the Levites by name, and verse 7 puts the ark on a cart. The men who should have been carrying it were standing in the crowd, watching it go by on wheels.

verseByVerse.quote: David consulted with the commanders of thousands and of hundreds, with every leader. And David said to all the assembly of Israel, "If it seems good to you and from the LORD our God, let us send abroad to our brothers who remain in all the lands of Israel, as well as to the priests and Levites in the cities that have pasturelands, that they may be gathered to us. Then let us bring again the ark of our God to us, for we did not seek it in the days of Saul."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The kingdom is barely a month old and David calls a council. Not about the Philistines, who are still in the land and will attack the moment they hear he has been crowned. Not about the treasury or the borders or the succession. About a box that has been sitting in a private house in the hills for twenty years.

He puts it to the assembly with two tests joined in one sentence: If it seems good to you and from the LORD our God. The people have to want it and God has to be in it, and he asks both questions in the same breath without ranking them. A king with a coronation behind him and 340,000 men at his back is asking permission.

Then the reason, and it is the sentence the Chronicler has been waiting three chapters to write. Then let us bring again the ark of our God to us, for we did not seek it in the days of Saul.

Saul's obituary had said the same word: he died because he broke faith and did not seek guidance from the LORD (10:13-14). Now the new king diagnoses forty years of national life in five words. Not that Saul persecuted the ark or forbade it. Nobody forbade it. It sat in Abinadab's house through a whole reign because no one got round to it, and a generation grew up in Israel who had never seen the throne of God.

That is what neglect looks like from inside. It is never a decision. There is no day on which Israel voted to leave the ark in the hills; there were simply twenty years of days on which nobody went to get it, and the first man to notice is the man who has just been made king.

verseByVerse.quote: All the assembly agreed to do so, for the thing was right in the eyes of all the people. So David assembled all Israel from the Nile of Egypt to Lebo-hamath, to bring the ark of God from Kiriath-jearim. And David and all Israel went up to Baalah, that is, to Kiriath-jearim that belongs to Judah, to bring up from there the ark of God, which is called by the name of the LORD who sits enthroned above the cherubim.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The assembly agrees, for the thing was right in the eyes of all the people, and David summons the nation from the Nile of Egypt to Lebo-hamath — the southern edge of the promise and the far northern pass, the whole territory God had described to Abraham and Moses, end to end.

The Chronicler's readers were a small community around one rebuilt town in a province of a foreign empire. Handing them a sentence with those two place names in it is not nostalgia. It is a map of what God said, laid over what they could see out of the window, and left there without comment.

Then the ark is described, and the description matters for everything that is about to happen. It is called by the name of the LORD who sits enthroned above the cherubim.

Not a relic. Not a national treasure with a history. A throne — a gold-covered lid with two winged figures facing each other across it, and the God of heaven seated between them. Everything that follows in this chapter depends on that clause being true, and everything that goes wrong in this chapter goes wrong because the men handling it were treating it as furniture.

verseByVerse.quote: And they carried the ark of God on a new cart, from the house of Abinadab, and Uzzah and Ahio were driving the cart. And David and all Israel were celebrating before God with all their might, with song and lyres and harps and tambourines and cymbals and trumpets.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they carried the ark of God on a new cart, from the house of Abinadab, and Uzzah and Ahio were driving the cart.

A new cart. It was clean, it was purpose-built, it was the best they had, and it was exactly what the Philistines had used. Twenty years earlier the lords of Ashdod had wanted the thing out of their country and their diviners told them to build a new cart and hitch two milk cows to it, and the ark had come back to Israel on wheels. Israel remembered how it arrived and copied the method, and nobody seems to have asked whether pagans who had no law were the right people to learn transport from.

Because there was a law, and it is specific. When the wagons were distributed at Sinai, two went to the sons of Gershon and four to the sons of Merari for the boards and hangings of the tabernacle. To the sons of Kohath, Moses gave none at all, because they were charged with the service of the holy things that had to be carried on the shoulder. And the same law said of the holy things: they must not touch them, or they will die.

So the wagon was not an oversight in the fine print. It was the one method God had expressly withheld, from the one family who might have been given it, for the one object now sitting on it. And David had already summoned the Levites in verse 2. They were somewhere in that procession, walking beside the cart.

Meanwhile the noise is tremendous — David and all Israel were celebrating before God with all their might, with song and lyres and harps and tambourines and cymbals and trumpets. Every word of that is sincere. Not one word of it is obedience, and the two are not the same thing.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At the threshing floor of Chidon the oxen stumble, Uzzah puts out his hand to steady the ark, and God strikes him down (vv. 9-10). He dies there before God, in the middle of the procession, with the music still playing. And David's first reaction is not reverence: David was angry because the LORD had broken out against Uzzah, and the place keeps the name Perez-uzza, the breaking out against Uzzah, ever after (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology: The verb behind the name is the one David will use himself in the next chapter, when God breaks through the Philistines for him like a bursting flood and he calls that place Baal-perazim. The same God breaks out both times. What changes between the two chapters is not God's character but whether Israel has troubled to find out how he said to come.
verseByVerse.examples: Uzzah reached out because the ark looked as though it might go down in the dirt. Underneath the reflex is an assumption: that the holiness of God needs a hand under it, and that someone had better keep it from embarrassment.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they came to the threshing floor of Chidon, Uzzah put out his hand to take hold of the ark, for the oxen stumbled. And the anger of the LORD was kindled against Uzzah, and he struck him down because he put out his hand to the ark, and he died there before God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Threshing floors are flat, open, exposed places on high ground, and the track up to one is rough. The oxen stumble. The cart lurches. And Uzzah, walking alongside, does what anyone would do: he puts out his hand.

Understand who he is. The ark had stood in his father Abinadab's house for something like twenty years. Uzzah had grown up in the same building as the throne of God. He had probably dusted around it as a boy. He is the last man in Israel who would have thought of it with terror, and that is precisely the problem: familiarity had worn the edge off the holiest object on earth, and his hand went out without a thought in it.

He was trying to help. That has to be said plainly, because the text does not soften it and neither should anyone else. He was not stealing and he was not scoffing. He reached out to stop the ark of God going down in the dirt in front of the whole nation.

And the anger of the LORD was kindled against Uzzah, and he struck him down because he put out his hand to the ark, and he died there before God.

Two things are going on and both have to be held. The first is the law: no hand touches this, and Uzzah's did. The second is larger, and David will state it himself in chapter 15 in the first person plural — we did not seek him according to the rule. The whole expedition was wrong before the oxen ever stumbled. Uzzah is the man who happened to be walking beside a cart that should never have existed, and the carelessness that killed him was the nation's before it was his.

What his reflex assumed is the thing to sit with. The ark was tilting, so a man put his hand under the holiness of God to keep it from falling. There is a whole way of handling sacred things buried in that gesture: the quiet conviction that God's honour depends on our management of it, that if we do not steady the situation something of his will be damaged. The God enthroned above the cherubim had not asked to be caught.

verseByVerse.quote: And David was angry because the LORD had broken out against Uzzah. And that place is called Perez-uzza to this day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And David was angry because the LORD had broken out against Uzzah.

Angry, and Scripture says it before it says anything else about him. The music has stopped, a man is lying dead on the road, the greatest day of the reign has collapsed, and the king is furious with God. The Chronicler had every opportunity to leave that clause out and did not.

He names the place for what happened there. Perez-uzza — the breaking out against Uzzah — and the name is still on the map when the book is written. Israel kept a marker on the spot where God had been terrible, and told the story to its children.

Now hold that verb, because it comes back almost immediately. In the very next chapter the Philistines come up against David and God gives him the victory, and David says: God has broken through my enemies by my hand, like a bursting flood. He calls that place Baal-perazim, the master of breakings-out. It is the same word. One chapter apart, the same God bursts out, and the first time it destroys a man on a cart track and the second time it scatters an army in front of the king.

The lesson is not that God is unpredictable. It is that there is one God with one kind of power, and Israel had been treating that power as manageable. A God who can break through an army like floodwater is not a God who can be carried about on a farm cart, and the same force that made David's enemies run is the force that went through Uzzah's arm when he reached out to help.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The anger turns to fear and the fear turns into a question: How can I bring the ark of God home to me? (v. 12). The procession halts. The ark is diverted to the house of Obed-edom the Gittite instead of into the city of David (v. 13), and stays there three months — during which the LORD blessed the household of Obed-edom and all that he had (v. 14).
verseByVerse.theology: The same ark that killed a man in the road blessed a household for a quarter of a year. Nothing about the ark changed in three months. The presence of God is not safe and is not hostile; it is holy, and how it meets a man is not a matter of chance.
verseByVerse.examples: David's question was a real question and it took him three months to answer it. When he comes back to the ark in chapter 15 he has found out what the rule was, and he says so out loud in front of everybody.

verseByVerse.quote: And David was afraid of God that day, and he said, "How can I bring the ark of God home to me?" So David did not take the ark home into the city of David, but took it aside to the house of Obed-edom the Gittite. And the ark of God remained with the household of Obed-edom in his house three months. And the LORD blessed the household of Obed-edom and all that he had.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The anger burns down into something better. And David was afraid of God that day, and he said, How can I bring the ark of God home to me?

It is a real question and it is the right one. Not why did you do that, but how am I to come to you. The king has just discovered that he does not know how to approach his own God, and rather than abandoning the project or repeating it louder he stops and asks. Fear of God, when it is the true kind, does not drive a man off. It makes him careful about the way in.

The answer took three months. He will come back for the ark in chapter 15 and the first thing he will say is that no one but the Levites may carry it, and the second is that they went wrong the first time because they did not seek God according to the rule. Somewhere in that quarter of a year David went and found out what had been written down for four hundred years, and it had been available the whole time.

Meanwhile the ark goes to a side road, to the house of Obed-edom the Gittite. He may have been a Philistine from Gath, or a Levite from Gath-rimmon, one of the towns given to the Levites in Joshua's day; the name will not settle it, and Chronicles later lists him among the gatekeepers of the sanctuary with sixty-two descendants and the note that God blessed him. Either way, the most dangerous object in the world is parked in his yard for three months because the king is afraid to take it home.

And the LORD blessed the household of Obed-edom and all that he had. Same ark. Same road, three months later. A man died beside it in the morning and a family prospered around it through a whole season, and nothing in the box had altered.

The lid Uzzah's hand touched had a name. It was the mercy seat, the place where blood was put once a year in the dark by one man who would not have survived going in without it. No hand touched that lid and lived. And the letter to the Romans says that God has taken the mercy seat and set it out in public, in the open street, in his Son — a propitiation put forward for all to see. What could not be touched has been displayed and offered. The hands that reached for Christ came away clean, and the leper he laid his hand on did not make him unclean but was made whole instead. Perez-uzza is a real place with a real grave in it, and the way home was opened by One who went to the holy God on our behalf and was himself broken out against, so that a household could be blessed.

13.theology:
Verse 3 carries the word the book is built around: we did not seek it in the days of Saul. Saul died because he did not seek the LORD (10:14); David begins by seeking him; and by chapter 15 David will have learned that seeking God is not only a matter of wanting to, but of coming the way he said — we did not seek him according to the rule (15:13). Sincerity was never in doubt in this chapter. Twenty thousand people were singing with all their might.

And the same verb runs through both halves of God's dealing with David. He broke out against Uzzah at Perez-uzza (v. 11) and he broke through the Philistines at Baal-perazim one chapter later (14:11). It is one God and one power. Israel's danger was never that God was weak; it was that they had grown used to him.
13.examples:
Uzzah had lived in the same house as the ark since he was a boy. The man who handled it most casually was the man who had been nearest it longest, and long familiarity with holy things is not the same as reverence for them. It is more often the thing that wears reverence away.

His hand went out to keep the ark from falling. Underneath that reflex lies the assumption that God's honour is fragile and depends on our steadying it — an assumption that shows up whenever people manage the truth to keep God from looking bad.

David was angry with God, and Scripture records it without excusing it or condemning it, and then records what the anger turned into: fear, a question, three months, and a man who came back having found out what he should have known. Anger at God is not the end of a life with him. What is done in the three months afterwards is the thing to watch.

14.title: David's House, Victories, and the Pattern of Seeking God
14.text: <sup>1</sup>And Hiram king of Tyre sent messengers to David, and cedar trees, also masons and carpenters to build a house for him.<sup>2</sup>And David knew that the LORD had established him as king over Israel, and that his kingdom was highly exalted for the sake of his people Israel.<sup>3</sup>And David took more wives in Jerusalem, and David fathered more sons and daughters.<sup>4</sup>These are the names of the children born to him in Jerusalem: Shammua, Shobab, Nathan, Solomon,<sup>5</sup>Ibhar, Elishua, Elpelet,<sup>6</sup>Nogah, Nepheg, Japhia,<sup>7</sup>Elishama, Beeliada and Eliphelet.<sup>8</sup>When the Philistines heard that David had been anointed king over all Israel, all the Philistines went up to search for David. But David heard of it and went out against them.<sup>9</sup>Now the Philistines had come and made a raid in the Valley of Rephaim.<sup>10</sup>And David inquired of God, "Shall I go up against the Philistines? Will you give them into my hand?" And the LORD said to him, "Go up, and I will give them into your hand."<sup>11</sup>And he went up to Baal-perazim, and David struck them down there. And David said, "God has broken through my enemies by my hand, like a bursting flood." Therefore the name of that place is called Baal-perazim.<sup>12</sup>And they left their gods there, and David gave command, and they were burned.<sup>13</sup>And the Philistines yet again made a raid in the valley.<sup>14</sup>And when David again inquired of God, God said to him, "You shall not go up after them; go around and come against them opposite the balsam trees.<sup>15</sup>And when you hear the sound of marching in the tops of the balsam trees, then go out to battle, for God has gone out before you to strike down the army of the Philistines."<sup>16</sup>And David did as God commanded him, and they struck down the Philistine army from Gibeon to Gezer.<sup>17</sup>And the fame of David went out into all lands, and the LORD brought the fear of him upon all nations.
14.overview:
Hiram of Tyre sends cedar and craftsmen and David reads the gift correctly (vv. 1-2); more wives are taken in Jerusalem and thirteen sons are listed, Nathan and Solomon among them (vv. 3-7); and the Philistines, provoked by the coronation, attack twice and are beaten twice (vv. 8-17).

The placing is the argument. In 2 Samuel this material stands before the ark narrative; the Chronicler has moved it into the gap between the failed attempt and the successful one, so that it falls in the three months while the ark sits at Obed-edom's. The king who did not seek God according to the rule in chapter 13 inquires twice here, and wins twice.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Hiram of Tyre sends cedar and craftsmen to build David a house (v. 1), and David draws the right conclusion from it: the LORD had established him as king over Israel, and ... his kingdom was highly exalted for the sake of his people Israel (v. 2). Then a plain sentence and a list — David took more wives in Jerusalem, and thirteen sons are named, among them Nathan and Solomon (vv. 3-4), down to Beeliada and Eliphelet (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: A superpower's embassy is the kind of thing that persuades a man he has arrived. David reads the cedar as evidence about somebody else: God put him there, and did it for the nation's sake rather than his own.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 3 is set down without a word of comment, and the law had said plainly that the king was not to multiply wives to himself. Amnon, Absalom and Adonijah are all in the house that this verse builds, and the Chronicler simply records it and moves on to the war.

verseByVerse.quote: And Hiram king of Tyre sent messengers to David, and cedar trees, also masons and carpenters to build a house for him. And David knew that the LORD had established him as king over Israel, and that his kingdom was highly exalted for the sake of his people Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Look first at where this chapter sits. In 2 Samuel, Hiram's cedar and the Philistine wars come before the ark is ever fetched. The Chronicler has lifted the whole block out and dropped it here, into the gap — into the three months while the ark stands in another man's yard and the king is afraid to go near it.

So the effect is deliberate. David's great project has stopped dead, a man is buried at Perez-uzza, and in that interval a Phoenician king sends him cedar and stonemasons, his family grows, and he beats the Philistines twice. God did not put the reign on hold while David worked out how to carry a box.

Tyre ran the richest port on that coast and dealt in the timber every great court in the world wanted. Its king sending a shipment of it inland to Jerusalem is a diplomatic judgement: the new man in the hills is worth an embassy.

And here is what David makes of it. David knew that the LORD had established him as king over Israel, and that his kingdom was highly exalted for the sake of his people Israel.

Both halves are unusual. He takes an international compliment as evidence about God rather than about himself — the LORD established him, and the timber is a receipt. And he takes his own exaltation as something aimed past him: the throne was raised for the sake of the nation standing under it. A man surrounded by cedar worked out that the cedar was not the point, and that he was not either.

Keep the cedar in view. Three chapters on, David will be sitting in the finished house and will suddenly find he cannot enjoy it, because the ark of the covenant is still under a tent.

verseByVerse.quote: And David took more wives in Jerusalem, and David fathered more sons and daughters. These are the names of the children born to him in Jerusalem: Shammua, Shobab, Nathan, Solomon, Ibhar, Elishua, Elpelet, Nogah, Nepheg, Japhia, Elishama, Beeliada and Eliphelet.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And David took more wives in Jerusalem, and David fathered more sons and daughters.

The Chronicler adds nothing. He does not defend it and he does not condemn it, and the law he knew perfectly well had said that a king must not multiply wives to himself, lest his heart turn away. This book leaves out the affair with Bathsheba altogether, and then prints this sentence, which is where the trouble in David's house actually starts. Amnon and Absalom and Adonijah are all born out of verse 3, and every one of them will tear the kingdom.

Then thirteen names, and two of them stand next to each other in verse 4. Nathan. Solomon.

Solomon is fourth on a routine list, with no star against him. The man who will build the temple this whole book is heading towards is entered here like any other child born in the capital that year. And beside him is a brother nobody remembers, whose line Luke traces when he comes to give the ancestry of Jesus — Matthew's genealogy comes down through Solomon and Luke's through Nathan, and both of them arrive at the same manger. Two names in one verse of a list, and the whole of the promise runs through the pair of them.

The last name but one is Beeliada, which means Baal knows, and in 2 Samuel the same son is called Eliada, God knows. Before Baal-worship poisoned the word, baal simply meant lord or master, and Israelites used it of the LORD without a qualm — one of the men who came to Ziklag two chapters back was called Bealiah, Yah is lord. A day came when the word could not be used at all, and God himself said through Hosea that his people would stop calling him my baal and call him my husband instead.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The coronation is what provokes the war: when the Philistines heard that David had been anointed king over all Israel, they came up to hunt him (v. 8). They raid the Valley of Rephaim, on Jerusalem's doorstep (v. 9). And David asks — Shall I go up against the Philistines? Will you give them into my hand? — and gets both answers back in his own words (v. 10). He wins, and names the place for the way God won it: God has broken through my enemies by my hand, like a bursting flood (v. 11). The Philistines run off and leave their gods on the field, and David has them burned (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: Chapter 10 ended with Saul's armour in the house of Dagon and the news carried round the Philistine temples. Here the idols are the ones left lying on a battlefield, and the king of Israel does with them exactly what the law had said to do with them.
verseByVerse.examples: David asked two questions, not one: may I go, and will you give them to me. He wanted permission and he wanted the outcome, and he was not willing to assume either of them from the fact that he had just been crowned.

verseByVerse.quote: When the Philistines heard that David had been anointed king over all Israel, all the Philistines went up to search for David. But David heard of it and went out against them. Now the Philistines had come and made a raid in the Valley of Rephaim. And David inquired of God, "Shall I go up against the Philistines? Will you give them into my hand?" And the LORD said to him, "Go up, and I will give them into your hand."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Philistines had left David alone for years. He had been a vassal of theirs at Ziklag and a useful nuisance to Saul, and a divided Israel suited them very well. Then: When the Philistines heard that David had been anointed king over all Israel, all the Philistines went up to search for David.

They come the moment he is crowned, and they come hunting a person. It is a compliment of a kind. The thing they had been happy to tolerate while Israel was in pieces has become intolerable now that a shepherd has the whole country behind him, and a united people under God's king is the one arrangement the enemies of God cannot live beside.

They raid the Valley of Rephaim, which runs south-west out of Jerusalem — close enough to see the walls from. And David, who could have moved on instinct because he had beaten these people all his life, stops and asks.

Shall I go up against the Philistines? Will you give them into my hand?

Two questions. Permission, and outcome. He will not presume that a crown is a licence to act, and he will not presume that a righteous cause guarantees a result. The last king had gone to a woman at Endor because heaven had stopped answering him; this one puts a plain question to God and gets a plain answer back in his own words: Go up, and I will give them into your hand.

verseByVerse.quote: And he went up to Baal-perazim, and David struck them down there. And David said, "God has broken through my enemies by my hand, like a bursting flood." Therefore the name of that place is called Baal-perazim. And they left their gods there, and David gave command, and they were burned.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The victory gets a sentence and the name of the place gets three. God has broken through my enemies by my hand, like a bursting flood.

The picture is a wadi wall giving way in a spring storm — water that has been building behind an obstruction until the obstruction is simply gone, and then everything downstream goes with it. David does not say he outfought them. He says God burst through, and adds by my hand, which is the whole doctrine of this book in four words: the flood was God's and the sword was his.

Now hear which word he has chosen. Breaking out is the word that was used three months ago about Uzzah, and the place where that happened is still called Perez-uzza. David had been angry at a God who breaks out. He now takes the same word, stands in a field of dead Philistines, and makes it a name to bless God by. Nothing about God had altered between the two hillsides. David had come to terms with him.

Then the detail. And they left their gods there, and David gave command, and they were burned. In chapter 10 the Philistines carried Saul's head into the house of their gods and sent the good news round their idols. Here the idols are lying face down in a valley where their people dropped them running, and the king of Israel does with them what the law of Moses had said to do: burn the carved images with fire. He got the ark wrong. He does not get this wrong. A man who has just been taught what obedience costs is careful with the next commandment he meets.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–17 — Wait for the Sound in the Trees
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Philistines come back to the same valley, and David does not repeat the manoeuvre that worked. He asks again, and this time the orders are different: You shall not go up after them; go around and come against them opposite the balsam trees (v. 14). The signal to attack is a sound in the treetops — for God has gone out before you to strike down the army of the Philistines (v. 15). David does as he is told, drives them from Gibeon to Gezer (v. 16), and the LORD brought the fear of him upon all nations (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology: Yesterday's answer is not today's orders. God had said go up once and says do not go up now, about the same enemy in the same field, and the only way to know that was to ask a second time.
verseByVerse.examples: The sound in the balsam trees is a signal nobody could manufacture, and it means the battle has already been won in front of him. David's part is to march out behind a host he cannot see and finish what was begun without him.

verseByVerse.quote: And the Philistines yet again made a raid in the valley. And when David again inquired of God, God said to him, "You shall not go up after them; go around and come against them opposite the balsam trees. And when you hear the sound of marching in the tops of the balsam trees, then go out to battle, for God has gone out before you to strike down the army of the Philistines."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They come back. Same enemy, same valley, and David has a proven method.

And when David again inquired of God — which is the most impressive word in the chapter. He had a divine mandate for this exact situation, three weeks old, and a battlefield named after the result. Repeating it would not have felt like presumption; it would have felt like faith. He asked anyway.

And the orders had changed. You shall not go up after them; go around and come against them opposite the balsam trees. Not up the valley this time but round behind, and then wait.

Wait for what? When you hear the sound of marching in the tops of the balsam trees, then go out to battle, for God has gone out before you to strike down the army of the Philistines.

The signal is a rustle overhead that sounds like men on the move — a sound no commander can arrange and no scout can fake, and which means that the God who broke out like a flood is already in the trees ahead of the infantry. By the time David's men step out of cover the fighting has begun without them. His whole task is to move when he hears it and finish what somebody else has started.

Two chapters ago the men gathering to a fugitive were described as an army like the army of God. Here the army of God is in the treetops going out ahead of them, and the only thing required of Israel is to keep step with a march they can hear and cannot see.

verseByVerse.quote: And David did as God commanded him, and they struck down the Philistine army from Gibeon to Gezer. And the fame of David went out into all lands, and the LORD brought the fear of him upon all nations.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And David did as God commanded him — six words that could not have been written about chapter 13 — and they struck down the Philistine army from Gibeon to Gezer. That is fifteen miles of pursuit, out of the hill country and down onto the coastal plain, which is to say they were driven off Israel's ridge entirely.

Then the last verse, and it does what the first two did. And the fame of David went out into all lands, and the LORD brought the fear of him upon all nations.

His name travelled; God carried the fear. The chapter opened with the LORD establishing him and closes with the LORD frightening the nations on his behalf, and everything in between — the cedar, the sons, the two victories — is set inside that pair of brackets. David asked twice and obeyed twice, and neither the asking nor the obeying is what made the Philistines run. God went out in front, in the tops of the trees, where nobody could see him and everybody could hear him coming.

14.theology:
Twice in ten verses David asks before he moves, and the second time is the one that matters. He had a fresh mandate for that precise situation and a battlefield named after the result, and he still asked — and was told to do something different. God's word to us yesterday is not a standing order for tomorrow.

The chapter is bracketed by God's action. The LORD had established him as king (v. 2); the LORD brought the fear of him upon all nations (v. 17). Inside those brackets David fights, and when he describes the victory he says God broke through by my hand (v. 11) — the same refusal to separate what God did from what the man did that ran through chapter 11.
14.examples:
An embassy from the richest court on the coast arrived with the finest timber in the world, and David concluded from it that God had put him where he was for somebody else's benefit. Success is read by everyone; what it is read as evidence of is the test.

Verse 3 records that the king took more wives, against an explicit command, and says nothing further. The sons of that verse will murder each other and rebel against their father. Scripture often reports a sin without comment and then lets the reader watch it grow up.

The word David chose at Baal-perazim was the word that had terrified him three months earlier at Perez-uzza. He did not avoid it. A man who has been frightened by God can come back and use the very same word to praise him.

15.title: The Ark Comes Right: Worship on God's Terms
15.text: <sup>1</sup>David built houses for himself in the city of David. And he prepared a place for the ark of God and pitched a tent for it.<sup>2</sup>Then David said that no one but the Levites may carry the ark of God, for the LORD had chosen them to carry the ark of the LORD and to minister to him forever.<sup>3</sup>And David assembled all Israel at Jerusalem to bring up the ark of the LORD to its place, which he had prepared for it.<sup>4</sup>And David gathered together the sons of Aaron and the Levites:<sup>5</sup>of the sons of Kohath, Uriel the chief, with 120 of his brothers;<sup>6</sup>of the sons of Merari, Asaiah the chief, with 220 of his brothers;<sup>7</sup>of the sons of Gershom, Joel the chief, with 130 of his brothers;<sup>8</sup>of the sons of Elizaphan, Shemaiah the chief, with 200 of his brothers;<sup>9</sup>of the sons of Hebron, Eliel the chief, with 80 of his brothers;<sup>10</sup>of the sons of Uzziel, Amminadab the chief, with 112 of his brothers.<sup>11</sup>Then David summoned the priests Zadok and Abiathar, and the Levites Uriel, Asaiah, Joel, Shemaiah, Eliel, and Amminadab,<sup>12</sup>and said to them, "You are the heads of the fathers' houses of the Levites. Consecrate yourselves, you and your brothers, so that you may bring up the ark of the LORD, the God of Israel, to the place that I have prepared for it.<sup>13</sup>Because you did not carry it the first time, the LORD our God broke out against us, because we did not seek him according to the rule."<sup>14</sup>So the priests and the Levites consecrated themselves to bring up the ark of the LORD, the God of Israel.<sup>15</sup>And the Levites carried the ark of God on their shoulders with the poles, as Moses had commanded according to the word of the LORD.<sup>16</sup>David also commanded the chiefs of the Levites to appoint their brothers as the singers who should play loudly on musical instruments, on harps and lyres and cymbals, to raise sounds of joy.<sup>17</sup>So the Levites appointed Heman the son of Joel; and of his brothers Asaph the son of Berechiah; and of the sons of Merari, their brothers, Ethan the son of Kushaiah;<sup>18</sup>and with them their brothers of the second order, Zechariah, Jaaziel, Shemiramoth, Jehiel, Unni, Eliab, Benaiah, Maaseiah, Mattithiah, Eliphelehu, and Mikneiah, and the gatekeepers Obed-edom and Jeiel.<sup>19</sup>The singers, Heman, Asaph, and Ethan, were to sound bronze cymbals;<sup>20</sup>Zechariah, Aziel, Shemiramoth, Jehiel, Unni, Eliab, Maaseiah, and Benaiah were to play harps according to Alamoth;<sup>21</sup>but Mattithiah, Eliphelehu, Mikneiah, Obed-edom, Jeiel, and Azaziah were to lead with lyres according to the Sheminith.<sup>22</sup>Chenaniah, leader of the Levites in music, should direct the music, for he understood it.<sup>23</sup>Berechiah and Elkanah were to be gatekeepers for the ark.<sup>24</sup>Shebaniah, Joshaphat, Nethanel, Amasai, Zechariah, Benaiah, and Eliezer, the priests, should blow the trumpets before the ark of God. Obed-edom and Jehiah were to be gatekeepers for the ark.<sup>25</sup>So David and the elders of Israel and the commanders of thousands went to bring up the ark of the covenant of the LORD from the house of Obed-edom with rejoicing.<sup>26</sup>And because God helped the Levites who were carrying the ark of the covenant of the LORD, they sacrificed seven bulls and seven rams.<sup>27</sup>David was clothed with a robe of fine linen, as also were all the Levites who were carrying the ark, and the singers and Chenaniah the leader of the music of the singers. And David wore a linen ephod.<sup>28</sup>So all Israel brought up the ark of the covenant of the LORD with shouting, to the sound of the horn, trumpets, and cymbals, and made loud music on harps and lyres.<sup>29</sup>And as the ark of the covenant of the LORD came to the city of David, Michal the daughter of Saul looked out of the window and saw King David dancing and celebrating, and she despised him in her heart.
15.overview:
David prepares a tent in Jerusalem and states the rule he has learned — only Levites may carry the ark (vv. 1-3). Six Levitical houses are mustered, 862 men (vv. 4-10); the priests and chiefs are told to consecrate themselves, and David confesses that the first attempt failed because we did not seek him according to the rule (vv. 11-15). Musicians and gatekeepers are appointed, Heman and Asaph and Ethan among them (vv. 16-24). Then the ark goes up with shouting and sacrifice, the king dressed in a Levite's linen (vv. 25-28) — and Michal the daughter of Saul watches from a window and despises him (v. 29).

The correction is not from loud worship to quiet worship. There is more music in this chapter than in chapter 13, and nine verses are spent arranging it. What changed is that somebody found out how God had said to come.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — This Time, According to the Rule
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David prepares a place in Jerusalem and pitches a tent for the ark (v. 1), and then states what he has learned: no one but the Levites may carry the ark of God, for the LORD had chosen them (v. 2). Six Levitical houses are mustered, 862 men in all (vv. 4-10). The priests Zadok and Abiathar and the six chiefs are summoned and told to consecrate themselves (vv. 11-12), and then David says out loud what went wrong: Because you did not carry it the first time, the LORD our God broke out against us, because we did not seek him according to the rule (v. 13). They consecrate themselves, and the ark goes up on their shoulders with the poles, as Moses had commanded according to the word of the LORD (vv. 14-15).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 13 is the book's key word turned back on the king who has been using it. Saul did not seek the LORD; David set out to seek him and found that wanting to was not enough. Seeking God includes coming the way he said to come, and David says so in the first person plural, with the man who died still fresh in everybody's memory.
verseByVerse.examples: He does not blame Uzzah and he does not blame God. He says we. A leader who can locate a disaster in his own decisions, out loud, in front of the men who carried it out, is rarer than a leader who can organise a procession.

verseByVerse.quote: David built houses for himself in the city of David. And he prepared a place for the ark of God and pitched a tent for it. Then David said that no one but the Levites may carry the ark of God, for the LORD had chosen them to carry the ark of the LORD and to minister to him forever. And David assembled all Israel at Jerusalem to bring up the ark of the LORD to its place, which he had prepared for it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three months have gone by. The ark is in another man's yard, the king has a question he could not answer, and the first thing verse 1 reports is that he built houses for himself.

Then: And he prepared a place for the ark of God and pitched a tent for it. The Chronicler puts the two clauses in that order and leaves them there. He is not scoring a point; he is telling the truth about how things get done, and the second clause is the one that cost David something to write.

The tent itself matters, because from this verse until Solomon's temple Israel has two sanctuaries. The tabernacle Moses made, with its bronze altar, is standing at Gibeon and will still be standing there at the end of the book. The ark is here, in a tent David pitched. The furniture of the covenant has been split between two hills for a generation, and it is Chronicles that tells us where the old one stood, which the books of Kings never say.

And then the sentence the whole chapter is built on. Then David said that no one but the Levites may carry the ark of God, for the LORD had chosen them to carry the ark of the LORD and to minister to him forever.

Somewhere in the three months he went and found out. The instruction had been in writing for four hundred years, unclassified, available to anyone who asked a priest. It is a strange thing that a man who could raise 340,000 soldiers and beat the Philistines twice needed a funeral to make him open the book, and it is not a strange thing at all, because that is usually the sequence.

And then, for the second time, David assembled all Israel at Jerusalem. He had done exactly that in chapter 13, from the Nile of Egypt to Lebo-hamath, and it had ended with a burial. He calls them out again. A man who has led a whole nation into a public disaster has to decide whether he will ever ask them to assemble for anything again, and David summons the same crowd back to the same road to watch him do it properly.

Note the reason he gives for the rule. Not that the Levites are safer or stronger, but that the LORD had chosen them. The ark travels on the shoulders of men God picked, and the point of the regulation was never crowd control. It was that God had said who.

verseByVerse.quote: And David gathered together the sons of Aaron and the Levites: of the sons of Kohath, Uriel the chief, with 120 of his brothers; of the sons of Merari, Asaiah the chief, with 220 of his brothers; of the sons of Gershom, Joel the chief, with 130 of his brothers; of the sons of Elizaphan, Shemaiah the chief, with 200 of his brothers; of the sons of Hebron, Eliel the chief, with 80 of his brothers; of the sons of Uzziel, Amminadab the chief, with 112 of his brothers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Six houses of Levi, counted out. Kohath 120 with Uriel at their head, Merari 220 under Asaiah, Gershom 130 under Joel, and then three clans from within Kohath — Elizaphan 200, Hebron 80, Uzziel 112.

Eight hundred and sixty-two men, named by family, with their chiefs. And verse 4 opens with a distinction the cart had erased: the sons of Aaron and the Levites. Priests and Levites are two orders with two kinds of work, and the first attempt had used neither.

Then look at which families are called. Kohath, Merari and Gershom are Levi's three sons, and all three are here — but the list does not stop there. Elizaphan and Hebron and Uzziel are Kohathite houses too, so four of the six contingents come from one branch of the family, and it is the branch the law had charged with the holy things themselves. When the wagons were handed out at Sinai, Gershon received two and Merari four and Kohath none at all, because what Kohath carried went on the shoulder.

So this is not a general call for volunteers with strong backs. David has gone to the exact clan the regulation named, and then summoned the rest of the tribe to walk with them.

Set that against chapter 13, where the transport arrangements were a cart, two oxen and two brothers. Nobody had been appointed. Nobody was responsible. The ark of the covenant of the LORD had gone up the road in the care of whoever happened to be walking beside it, and the whole nation was singing.

The difference here is not zeal; there was no shortage of zeal at Chidon. The difference is that this time somebody worked out who God had said should do the job, went and found them, and wrote down their names. Eight hundred and sixty-two men had to be identified and summoned and put in order before the ark moved a yard, and the Chronicler records the arithmetic because the arithmetic is the repentance.

verseByVerse.quote: Then David summoned the priests Zadok and Abiathar, and the Levites Uriel, Asaiah, Joel, Shemaiah, Eliel, and Amminadab, and said to them, "You are the heads of the fathers' houses of the Levites. Consecrate yourselves, you and your brothers, so that you may bring up the ark of the LORD, the God of Israel, to the place that I have prepared for it. Because you did not carry it the first time, the LORD our God broke out against us, because we did not seek him according to the rule."
verseByVerse.commentary:
David sends for the two high priests and the six Levite chiefs. Zadok is here — the young man with a sword and twenty-two officers from chapter 12, now standing at the head of the priesthood — and beside him Abiathar, the one man who got out of Nob alive when Saul had eighty-five priests killed in a morning. Two survivors of two very different disasters, summoned to handle the ark.

Consecrate yourselves, you and your brothers, so that you may bring up the ark of the LORD, the God of Israel, to the place that I have prepared for it.

And then verse 13, which is the sentence this whole part of the book has been moving towards.

Because you did not carry it the first time, the LORD our God broke out against us, because we did not seek him according to the rule.

Take it in pieces, because every clause is doing work. You did not carry it — the Levites are told, to their faces, that the failure was theirs too; the men who knew the law had stood by and watched the cart go past. The LORD our God broke out against us — the same verb as Perez-uzza and Baal-perazim, and this time the object is not Uzzah but us. And then the confession itself: we did not seek him according to the rule.

That is the word this book keeps returning to. Saul died because he did not seek the LORD. David's first act as king was to say let us go and seek him, and he was right to say it, and a man died anyway. Now he can finish the sentence. Seeking God is not only a matter of wanting him badly enough. It includes finding out how he has said to come and then coming that way, and the difference between those two things had cost a life.

What he does not say is as striking as what he does. He does not say Uzzah was careless. He does not say the oxen stumbled. He does not say God was severe, though three months earlier he had been angry enough to think it.
