He says we, standing in front of the men who did the carrying, before a nation that had watched it happen, and then gets on with the arrangements.

verseByVerse.quote: So the priests and the Levites consecrated themselves to bring up the ark of the LORD, the God of Israel. And the Levites carried the ark of God on their shoulders with the poles, as Moses had commanded according to the word of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So the priests and the Levites consecrated themselves to bring up the ark of the LORD, the God of Israel.

Consecration meant washing, laundering, abstaining, and putting a distance between yourself and ordinary life for a set time. It is slow and it is unglamorous and none of it shows in a procession. The men who were going to touch the poles spent days making themselves fit to do it, and the crowd would never know.

Then verse 15, and the Chronicler writes it with unusual care. And the Levites carried the ark of God on their shoulders with the poles, as Moses had commanded according to the word of the LORD.

Shoulders. Poles. The two rings on each side of the ark had held those poles since the day it was made, and the poles were never to be taken out. Everything needed for carrying it correctly had been attached to it the whole time, including on the day it rode a cart.

And the authority is stated twice over: as Moses commanded, according to the word of the LORD. Not Moses' opinion about transport. The Chronicler is writing for people who might think that an old book of regulations is a lower order of thing than a living encounter with God, and he sets the two clauses side by side to say that they are the same clause.

Human shoulders. Not wheels, not oxen, not a machine — the throne of God moved through Israel on the backs of men who had made themselves ready for it. Centuries later the Word who dwelt above those cherubim would come down into the world carried by a girl, and go up the last hill of his life with a beam on his own shoulder.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before the ark moves, the music is organised. David tells the chiefs of the Levites to appoint singers with harps and lyres and cymbals to raise sounds of joy (v. 16). Three names head the list — Heman, Asaph and Ethan on bronze cymbals (vv. 17-19) — with a second order behind them on harps and lyres tuned two different ways (vv. 20-21). Chenaniah directs, for he understood it (v. 22); gatekeepers are set for the ark itself; and seven priests are to blow the trumpets in front of it (vv. 23-24).
verseByVerse.theology: Joy is being arranged. Nine verses of appointments stand between the confession and the procession, and the Chronicler thinks they belong in Scripture. Worship that is careful about God's word turns out to be worship with more music in it, not less.
verseByVerse.examples: Obed-edom's name is in this list twice. The ark had stood in his house for three months and his household had been blessed for it, and when it moved he went with it and took a doorkeeper's post.

verseByVerse.quote: David also commanded the chiefs of the Levites to appoint their brothers as the singers who should play loudly on musical instruments, on harps and lyres and cymbals, to raise sounds of joy. So the Levites appointed Heman the son of Joel; and of his brothers Asaph the son of Berechiah; and of the sons of Merari, their brothers, Ethan the son of Kushaiah; and with them their brothers of the second order, Zechariah, Jaaziel, Shemiramoth, Jehiel, Unni, Eliab, Benaiah, Maaseiah, Mattithiah, Eliphelehu, and Mikneiah, and the gatekeepers Obed-edom and Jeiel. The singers, Heman, Asaph, and Ethan, were to sound bronze cymbals;
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ark has not moved yet. Before it does, David appoints the choir.

David also commanded the chiefs of the Levites to appoint their brothers as the singers who should play loudly on musical instruments, on harps and lyres and cymbals, to raise sounds of joy.

Loudly, and joy. There is a way of reading chapter 13 that concludes the lesson was to be more solemn, and this verse forbids it. The correction was never from noise to quiet. Nine verses of this chapter are spent organising music, which is more space than the Chronicler gives to the carrying itself, and the whole aim of the appointments is stated as raising sounds of joy. Getting the rule right is what made the shouting safe.

Then three names on the cymbals: Heman, Asaph and Ethan.

Asaph's name stands over a dozen psalms still sung today — the one that begins with God summoning heaven and earth to judgement, and the one that admits that a man nearly lost his footing over how well the wicked were doing. The titles of two more psalms name a Heman and an Ethan: the darkest prayer in the book, which ends with the word darkness, and the long meditation on God's covenant with David that asks how long the promise will lie in ruins.

There is an arrangement in the three of them that the text half states and chapter 6 finishes. That chapter traced Heman's line back to Kohath and Asaph's to Gershom, and this verse says outright that Ethan is of the sons of Merari. One chief musician from each of Levi's three sons, standing side by side on the cymbals. No branch of that family was left out of the noise.

Behind them a second order of eleven, listed one by one — Zechariah, Jaaziel, Shemiramoth, Jehiel, Unni, Eliab, Benaiah, Maaseiah, Mattithiah, Eliphelehu, Mikneiah. Second-rank players, written into Scripture by name. Three men are remembered for the cymbals; these eleven were the sound.

They are appointed here as instrumentalists for one afternoon's procession. Nobody in that street knew that the men on the cymbals were being handed a job that would outlast the city, and that Israel would still be praying their words in a foreign country five hundred years later.

verseByVerse.quote: Zechariah, Aziel, Shemiramoth, Jehiel, Unni, Eliab, Maaseiah, and Benaiah were to play harps according to Alamoth; but Mattithiah, Eliphelehu, Mikneiah, Obed-edom, Jeiel, and Azaziah were to lead with lyres according to the Sheminith. Chenaniah, leader of the Levites in music, should direct the music, for he understood it. Berechiah and Elkanah were to be gatekeepers for the ark. Shebaniah, Joshaphat, Nethanel, Amasai, Zechariah, Benaiah, and Eliezer, the priests, should blow the trumpets before the ark of God. Obed-edom and Jehiah were to be gatekeepers for the ark.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the technical detail, and it is technical. One group plays harps according to Alamoth and another leads with lyres according to the Sheminith — most likely a higher register and a lower one, two settings kept distinct so that the sound had structure instead of volume alone. Those two words are still standing in the titles of psalms, which means somebody kept the performance notes.

And a director is appointed. Chenaniah, leader of the Levites in music, should direct the music, for he understood it.

He got the post because he knew what he was doing. Scripture states the qualification plainly and does not add a word about his piety, which is not a slight on piety; it is a recognition that leading a hundred musicians is a competence, and that a consecrated man who cannot hear a wrong entry is not the man for it. The same chapter that insists on doing things God's way insists on putting someone in charge who understands the job.

Then the doorkeepers, and one name in the list should stop a reader. The gatekeepers Obed-edom and Jeiel. He is there again at verse 21 with a lyre and again at verse 24 on the door.

Two more doorkeepers are posted in verse 23, Berechiah and Elkanah, stationed at the ark itself. Somebody had to stand between the crowd and the thing that had killed a man, and the post was given names and an order rather than left to whoever happened to be nearest — which is exactly what it had been left to at the threshing floor.

Then the trumpets. Shebaniah, Joshaphat, Nethanel, Amasai, Zechariah, Benaiah, and Eliezer, the priests, should blow the trumpets before the ark of God.

Seven priests, out in front. Trumpets are not an ordinary instrument in Israel; they are the one piece of music God specified himself. He told Moses to make two of hammered silver and said exactly when they were to sound: to call the congregation together, to move the camp, to go out to war so that Israel would be remembered before the LORD, and on the day of your gladness, over the burnt offerings. Every one of those occasions is happening at once on this road. The camp is on the move, the congregation is assembled, the sacrifices are burning, and nobody could mistake the gladness.

So the column that goes up the hill has priests with silver trumpets at its head, Levites with the poles on their shoulders behind them, three houses of Levi on the cymbals, eleven more on the strings, doorkeepers walking beside the ark, a director who understood music, and a king dressed like a porter. Not one of those posts existed in chapter 13.

This is the man from whose house the ark is about to be taken. It had stood in his property for three months and his family had been blessed every day of it, and now the king arrives with 862 Levites to carry it away to the capital. He could have watched it go. Instead he put on linen and took a post at the door, and walked to Jerusalem beside it. Ten chapters later his descendants are still on the temple roster, sixty-two of them, with a note beside the name that says God blessed him.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David and the elders and the commanders go down to fetch the ark from Obed-edom's house with rejoicing (v. 25). Because God helped the Levites who were carrying the ark, seven bulls and seven rams are sacrificed (v. 26). The king is dressed in fine linen, the same as every Levite carrying the ark, with a linen ephod (v. 27), and all Israel brings it up with shouting and horns and cymbals (v. 28). And in the last verse Michal the daughter of Saul watches from a window and despises him (v. 29).
verseByVerse.theology: The sacrifice in verse 26 is a thank-offering for being kept alive. Nobody in that procession had forgotten what happened at the threshing floor, and the note the Chronicler makes is that God helped the men doing the carrying.
verseByVerse.examples: The chapter ends looking up at a window. Everyone in the street is shouting and one person is watching, and Scripture identifies her not as David's wife but as Saul's daughter.

verseByVerse.quote: So David and the elders of Israel and the commanders of thousands went to bring up the ark of the covenant of the LORD from the house of Obed-edom with rejoicing. And because God helped the Levites who were carrying the ark of the covenant of the LORD, they sacrificed seven bulls and seven rams.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the road. So David and the elders of Israel and the commanders of thousands went to bring up the ark of the covenant of the LORD from the house of Obed-edom with rejoicing.

Same road as last time. Same ark. Same king, and a good many of the same people, walking past a place with a grave in it and a name that meant the breaking out against Uzzah.

And then a clause that only makes sense if you remember why they were frightened: because God helped the Levites who were carrying the ark of the covenant of the LORD, they sacrificed seven bulls and seven rams.

God helped the carriers. That is the reason given for the sacrifice, and it means the men under the poles got to the end of the journey alive and knew perfectly well that this was not a foregone conclusion. Fourteen animals were killed in thanksgiving for a walk completed. Doing the right thing in the right way had not made these men casual about being near God; it had simply made it possible to be near him.

Helping is the word this part of the book keeps using. Men came to David to help him, and the Spirit told him that his God helped him, and now God helps the men carrying the throne of God up a hill. Every one of them had two hands on a pole and every one of them was being held.

verseByVerse.quote: David was clothed with a robe of fine linen, as also were all the Levites who were carrying the ark, and the singers and Chenaniah the leader of the music of the singers. And David wore a linen ephod. So all Israel brought up the ark of the covenant of the LORD with shouting, to the sound of the horn, trumpets, and cymbals, and made loud music on harps and lyres.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David was clothed with a robe of fine linen, as also were all the Levites who were carrying the ark, and the singers and Chenaniah the leader of the music of the singers. And David wore a linen ephod.

Read the clothing list again and notice who is not distinguished. The king is in the same fine linen as the porters and the choir. He has come out in the uniform of the men doing the lifting, and over it he has put an ephod — which is not royal dress at all. It is what a priest wore, and what the boy Samuel wore in the sanctuary at Shiloh.

He is not seizing the priesthood; a later king of Judah tried that with a censer in his hand and came out of the temple a leper. He is doing something else, and it is deliberate. On the day the throne of God enters his capital, David takes off the clothes that mark him out from everyone else and dresses like a servant of the sanctuary.

Then the sound. So all Israel brought up the ark of the covenant of the LORD with shouting, to the sound of the horn, trumpets, and cymbals, and made loud music on harps and lyres. Everything chapter 13 had, and one thing more.

There is a night in an upper room when the Lord of glory got up from supper, laid aside his outer garments, tied a towel round himself and washed the feet of the men who were about to abandon him. David in linen at the head of a procession is a small picture of a very great one, and the greater one did not put the robe back on until he had died.

verseByVerse.quote: And as the ark of the covenant of the LORD came to the city of David, Michal the daughter of Saul looked out of the window and saw King David dancing and celebrating, and she despised him in her heart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter ends at a window.

And as the ark of the covenant of the LORD came to the city of David, Michal the daughter of Saul looked out of the window and saw King David dancing and celebrating, and she despised him in her heart.

She is called the daughter of Saul. She had been David's wife since he brought Saul two hundred Philistine foreskins for her, and she had let him down through a window once before to save his life. The Chronicler gives none of that. He gives her father's name, and the reader who has come through chapter 10 knows exactly what that means: the house that did not seek the ark in the days of Saul is watching the ark arrive.

2 Samuel tells the rest — the row in the doorway, her sarcasm about how the king of Israel had exposed himself before the servant girls, his answer that he would be more contemptible than this, and the flat note that she had no child to the day of her death. The Chronicler cuts it all. He stops at four words: she despised him in her heart. Nothing was said. Nobody in the street knew. The contempt stayed inside and it was complete already.

Look at the two vantage points the verse gives. Down in the road there is a king in a linen tunic with no crown on, shouting, out of breath, in the middle of a crowd, going up the hill with the poles ahead of him. Up in the house there is a window, and a person standing at it with her arms folded, and everything she was raised to value telling her that what she is looking at is beneath the dignity of a throne.

She was not wrong about the dignity. That was the whole point of the linen. What she could not see from a window was that the man dancing in the street had understood something her father never did: that when God comes to live among his people there is no dignity worth keeping that would stop a man from going out to meet him.

15.theology:
Verse 13 finishes a sentence the book began at 10:14. Saul died because he did not seek the LORD. David's answer was to go and seek him — and a man died, because wanting God is not the same as coming to God the way he has said. We did not seek him according to the rule. The remedy was not less enthusiasm; it was the book of Moses, read, and eight hundred and sixty-two men called by name.

Verse 15 sets two authorities side by side as one: as Moses had commanded according to the word of the LORD. A written regulation four centuries old and the living word of God are not two different classes of thing. And in verse 26, the God whose rule they finally kept is the one who helped the Levites who were carrying the ark — obedience did not put them beyond needing help; it put them where help was given.
15.examples:
David confessed in the first person plural, in front of the men who had carried out his instructions, and named the exact fault. He did not blame Uzzah, or the oxen, or God. Then he organised the thing properly and got on with it, which is what repentance looks like when it has stopped talking.

Chenaniah was put in charge of the music because he understood music. Competence is treated here as a genuine qualification and not a worldly intrusion, and a chapter obsessed with doing things God's way is the chapter that says so.

Obed-edom had the ark taken out of his own house and joined the procession as a doorkeeper. A blessing that moves on somewhere else can be followed rather than mourned, and his family were still serving at those doors generations later.

16.title: The Psalm of Praise: The Ark at Rest and the Song That Fills the Earth
16.text: <sup>1</sup>And they brought in the ark of God and set it inside the tent that David had pitched for it, and they offered burnt offerings and peace offerings before God.<sup>2</sup>And when David had finished offering the burnt offerings and the peace offerings, he blessed the people in the name of the LORD<sup>3</sup>and distributed to all Israel, both men and women, to each a loaf of bread, a portion of meat, and a cake of raisins.<sup>4</sup>Then he appointed some of the Levites as ministers before the ark of the LORD, to invoke, to thank, and to praise the LORD, the God of Israel.<sup>5</sup>Asaph was the chief, and second to him were Zechariah, Jeiel, Shemiramoth, Jehiel, Mattithiah, Eliab, Benaiah, Obed-edom, and Jeiel, who were to play harps and lyres; Asaph was to sound the cymbals,<sup>6</sup>and Benaiah and Jahaziel the priests were to blow trumpets regularly before the ark of the covenant of God.<sup>7</sup>Then on that day David first appointed that thanksgiving be sung to the LORD by Asaph and his brothers.<sup>8</sup>Oh give thanks to the LORD; call upon his name; make known his deeds among the peoples!<sup>9</sup>Sing to him, sing praises to him; tell of all his wondrous works!<sup>10</sup>Glory in his holy name; let the hearts of those who seek the LORD rejoice!<sup>11</sup>Seek the LORD and his strength; seek his presence continually!<sup>12</sup>Remember the wondrous works that he has done, his miracles and the judgments he uttered,<sup>13</sup>O offspring of Israel his servant, children of Jacob, his chosen ones!<sup>14</sup>He is the LORD our God; his judgments are in all the earth.<sup>15</sup>Remember his covenant forever, the word that he commanded, for a thousand generations,<sup>16</sup>the covenant that he made with Abraham, his sworn promise to Isaac,<sup>17</sup>which he confirmed to Jacob as a statute, to Israel as an everlasting covenant,<sup>18</sup>saying, "To you I will give the land of Canaan, as your portion for an inheritance."<sup>19</sup>When you were few in number, of little account, and sojourners in it,<sup>20</sup>wandering from nation to nation, from one kingdom to another people,<sup>21</sup>he allowed no one to oppress them; he rebuked kings on their account,<sup>22</sup>saying, "Touch not my anointed ones, do my prophets no harm!"<sup>23</sup>Sing to the LORD, all the earth! Tell of his salvation from day to day.<sup>24</sup>Declare his glory among the nations, his marvelous works among all the peoples!<sup>25</sup>For great is the LORD, and greatly to be praised, and he is to be feared above all gods.<sup>26</sup>For all the gods of the peoples are worthless idols, but the LORD made the heavens.<sup>27</sup>Splendor and majesty are before him; strength and joy are in his place.<sup>28</sup>Ascribe to the LORD, O families of the peoples, ascribe to the LORD glory and strength!<sup>29</sup>Ascribe to the LORD the glory due his name; bring an offering and come before him! Worship the LORD in the splendor of holiness;<sup>30</sup>tremble before him, all the earth; yes, the world is established; it shall never be moved.<sup>31</sup>Let the heavens be glad, and let the earth rejoice, and let them say among the nations, "The LORD reigns!"<sup>32</sup>Let the sea roar, and all that fills it; let the field exult, and everything in it!<sup>33</sup>Then shall the trees of the forest sing for joy before the LORD, for he comes to judge the earth.<sup>34</sup>Oh give thanks to the LORD, for he is good; for his steadfast love endures forever!<sup>35</sup>Say also: "Save us, O God of our salvation, and gather and deliver us from among the nations, that we may give thanks to your holy name and glory in your praise.<sup>36</sup>Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, from everlasting to everlasting!" Then all the people said, "Amen!" and praised the LORD.<sup>37</sup>So David left Asaph and his brothers there before the ark of the covenant of the LORD to minister regularly before the ark as each day required,<sup>38</sup>and also Obed-edom and his sixty-eight brothers, while Obed-edom, the son of Jeduthun, and Hosah were to be gatekeepers.<sup>39</sup>And he left Zadok the priest and his brothers the priests before the tabernacle of the LORD in the high place that was at Gibeon<sup>40</sup>to offer burnt offerings to the LORD on the altar of burnt offering regularly morning and evening, to do all that is written in the Law of the LORD that he commanded Israel.<sup>41</sup>With them were Heman and Jeduthun and the rest of those chosen and expressly named to give thanks to the LORD, for his steadfast love endures forever.<sup>42</sup>Heman and Jeduthun had trumpets and cymbals for the music and instruments for sacred song. The sons of Jeduthun were appointed to the gate.<sup>43</sup>Then all the people departed each to his house, and David went home to bless his household.
16.overview:
The ark is set in the tent and offerings are made; David blesses the people and gives a loaf, a portion of meat and a raisin cake to every person present, men and women alike (vv. 1-3). A permanent order of Levitical musicians is created (vv. 4-6), and on that day thanksgiving is first appointed to be sung (v. 7). The psalm follows in three movements: remember the covenant with Abraham (vv. 8-22), sing to the LORD all the earth (vv. 23-33), and give thanks, for his steadfast love endures forever (vv. 34-36). Then the standing arrangements — the ark and the choir in Jerusalem, the tabernacle and the altar at Gibeon (vv. 37-42) — and everyone goes home (v. 43).

The psalm is a composite of Psalm 105, Psalm 96 and Psalm 106, and its shape is deliberate: memory, then mission, then hope. Israel's worship starts on the day it is given all three.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — The Ark at Rest, and a Loaf for Everybody
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The ark is set inside the tent and burnt offerings and peace offerings are made (v. 1). David blesses the people in the LORD's name and hands out to all Israel, both men and women, to each a loaf of bread, a portion of meat, and a cake of raisins (vv. 2-3). Then a permanent office is created: Levites stationed before the ark to invoke, to thank, and to praise the LORD, Asaph at their head, with priests blowing trumpets regularly (vv. 4-6). And verse 7 dates it — on that day David first appointed that thanksgiving be sung to the LORD by Asaph and his brothers.
verseByVerse.theology: The peace offering was the one sacrifice the worshipper ate, and verse 3 is what that looked like at national scale: every person in the crowd going home with meat in their hands from the king's table. Worship at the ark did not end in awe alone. It ended in a meal, and nobody was left out of it.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 7 is a founding date. Israel had sung before, but from this afternoon there were men whose job was thanksgiving, on a rota, every day, whether anyone was watching or not.

verseByVerse.quote: And they brought in the ark of God and set it inside the tent that David had pitched for it, and they offered burnt offerings and peace offerings before God. And when David had finished offering the burnt offerings and the peace offerings, he blessed the people in the name of the LORD and distributed to all Israel, both men and women, to each a loaf of bread, a portion of meat, and a cake of raisins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they brought in the ark of God and set it inside the tent that David had pitched for it.

Set it down. After Shiloh, after the Philistine capture and the tumours and the cart with the lowing cows, after twenty years in a private house on a hill, after a death on a threshing floor and three months in a Gittite's yard — the throne of God is set down in a tent in the capital, and the poles are put on the ground, and the men who carried it straighten up.

Two kinds of offering follow, and they are not the same thing. A burnt offering went up entirely in smoke; nobody ate any of it. A peace offering was shared — part burned, part to the priest, and the rest eaten by the worshipper and his family on the spot, in front of God. One says everything here is yours. The other says come and eat with me.

Then David blesses the people in the name of the LORD, which is what Aaron's sons were commissioned to do, and does something that follows straight out of the peace offering.

And distributed to all Israel, both men and women, to each a loaf of bread, a portion of meat, and a cake of raisins.

To each. Every person in that crowd, and the text goes out of its way to say men and women, which it did not have to say. Not the elders, not the commanders of thousands, not the Levites who had done the work. A woman standing at the back of a national assembly went home with bread and meat and a cake of pressed raisins in her hands, given her by the king, off the altar of God.

That is what the day of the ark's arrival looked like at ground level. Not a policy and not a doctrine — a hand held out with food in it, to everyone, without a list. And it is what the whole thing has always been driving at, because the God who came to live among his people set a table when he came, and the last picture Scripture gives of the finished work is a supper with a seat for every nation.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he appointed some of the Levites as ministers before the ark of the LORD, to invoke, to thank, and to praise the LORD, the God of Israel. Asaph was the chief, and second to him were Zechariah, Jeiel, Shemiramoth, Jehiel, Mattithiah, Eliab, Benaiah, Obed-edom, and Jeiel, who were to play harps and lyres; Asaph was to sound the cymbals, and Benaiah and Jahaziel the priests were to blow trumpets regularly before the ark of the covenant of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then something new is invented. He appointed some of the Levites as ministers before the ark of the LORD, to invoke, to thank, and to praise the LORD, the God of Israel.

Three verbs, and they are the job description. To invoke is to bring God's acts to remembrance out loud. To thank is to name what he has done as a gift. To praise is to say what he is like because he is like it. That is the whole of a worship service in three words, and from this day it is somebody's occupation.

Nothing in the law of Moses had said anything about this. The regulations were about blood and bread and incense and the fabric of a tent; there is no order of singers in the book of Leviticus. David reads what has been commanded, obeys it exactly, and then adds a permanent choir, and the Chronicler is entirely happy about it. Getting the rule right at the threshing floor did not turn David into a man who would only ever do what was on the list.

Asaph is the chief. Behind him nine players on harps and lyres, including Obed-edom again, and Asaph himself on the cymbals. And two priests, Benaiah and Jahaziel, to blow trumpets regularly before the ark of the covenant of God.

Regularly. The trumpets that had sounded in front of the procession are not put away when the excitement is over. Someone will blow them tomorrow, and the day after, and on the wet Tuesday in February when there is no crowd. The most striking word in the paragraph is the dullest one in it.

verseByVerse.quote: Then on that day David first appointed that thanksgiving be sung to the LORD by Asaph and his brothers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then on that day David first appointed that thanksgiving be sung to the LORD by Asaph and his brothers.

A date. The Chronicler is telling his readers when the thing they do every day in the temple began, and it began on the afternoon the ark came home.

What follows is the psalm they sang, and anyone who reads the Psalter will recognise it. The first movement is the opening of Psalm 105. The middle is almost the whole of Psalm 96. The end is the first verse and the last two verses of Psalm 106. It is a composite, assembled out of three songs — or three songs that grew from it. Which way the borrowing ran cannot be settled from here, and it does not need to be.

What can be seen is the shape somebody gave it, and the shape is deliberate. It looks backwards, then outwards, then forwards: remember what God swore to your fathers; tell the nations who is on the throne; and gather us home. Past, world, future. Israel's worship began the day it was given a memory, a mission and a hope, in that order.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–22 — Remember: the Covenant with Abraham
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The first movement of the psalm is memory. Give thanks, call on his name, make his deeds known among the peoples (v. 8); glory in his holy name, and — three times in two verses — seek the LORD and his strength; seek his presence continually (vv. 10-11). Then the covenant itself: remember it forever, the word he commanded for a thousand generations, made with Abraham, sworn to Isaac, confirmed to Jacob (vv. 15-17), with the land as its content (v. 18). And the state the patriarchs were in when he made it: few in number, of little account, and sojourners, wandering between kingdoms, with God rebuking kings on their account and saying Touch not my anointed ones (vv. 19-22).
verseByVerse.theology: The verbs at verses 10 and 11 are the word the whole book turns on, and here the object changes. Saul did not seek the LORD. David sought the ark and got it wrong, then sought God according to the rule and got it right. Now the congregation is told to seek his face, and to keep on seeking it after they have found it.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 19 says you where the psalm in the Psalter says they. A community that was few in number and of little account is being handed the patriarchs' own description of themselves and told that God made an everlasting covenant with people in exactly that condition.

verseByVerse.quote: Oh give thanks to the LORD; call upon his name; make known his deeds among the peoples! Sing to him, sing praises to him; tell of all his wondrous works! Glory in his holy name; let the hearts of those who seek the LORD rejoice! Seek the LORD and his strength; seek his presence continually! Remember the wondrous works that he has done, his miracles and the judgments he uttered, O offspring of Israel his servant, children of Jacob, his chosen ones!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The opening is a stack of imperatives with the nations already in view. Give thanks, call on his name, and then: make known his deeds among the peoples. Six lines in, on the day a tent was pitched on a Judean ridge, the congregation is told that what has happened to them is news for everybody else.

Verse 9 puts three verbs together and two of them are singing: Sing to him, sing praises to him; tell of all his wondrous works! The third is the one people find hardest. Telling is not performance and not liturgy; it is talking about what God has done, out loud, to someone, in the ordinary way one person tells another a piece of news.

Then verses 10 and 11, which are the middle of this book's argument.

Glory in his holy name; let the hearts of those who seek the LORD rejoice! Seek the LORD and his strength; seek his presence continually!

Three times, seek. It is the word the book has been carrying since the obituary in chapter 10, where Saul died because he did not seek the LORD, and it has been changing its object each time it appears. In chapter 13 David wanted to seek it — the ark, the object, the thing they had neglected. In chapter 15 he had learned to seek him according to the rule. Here it is neither a relic nor a regulation. Seek his presence continually — literally, seek his face.

That is the destination the whole sequence was travelling to. A man can seek an object and get it into a tent. A man can seek a rule and keep it exactly. Neither of those is the same as wanting the face of God, and David has been taken through both to arrive at the third.

And then the word continually, which quietly rules out the obvious mistake. The ark has just been found. The searching is over; the thing has arrived and is twenty yards away behind a curtain. And the command is to go on seeking, every day, for ever. Whatever it means to have God, it does not mean the seeking stops.

Verse 12 takes the phrase from verse 9 and turns it inward: Remember the wondrous works that he has done, his miracles and the judgments he uttered. The same wondrous works are to be told to outsiders and remembered by insiders, and a congregation that stops doing the second will very soon have nothing to do the first with.

And a word enters here that will not leave the psalm: the judgments he uttered. It comes again two verses later — his judgments are in all the earth — and once more at the very end, where the trees sing because he comes to judge the earth. Three times, and the movement is from what he has said, to what he is doing everywhere, to what he is coming to do. It is one continuous action, and the psalm treats all three tenses of it as grounds for singing.

The congregation is addressed by name in verse 13: O offspring of Israel his servant, children of Jacob, his chosen ones. Not achievers. Chosen ones, and the son of a man who spent his life being carried by God rather than impressing him.

verseByVerse.quote: He is the LORD our God; his judgments are in all the earth. Remember his covenant forever, the word that he commanded, for a thousand generations, the covenant that he made with Abraham, his sworn promise to Isaac, which he confirmed to Jacob as a statute, to Israel as an everlasting covenant, saying, "To you I will give the land of Canaan, as your portion for an inheritance."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He is the LORD our God; his judgments are in all the earth. Ours, and in all the earth — a particular God with a universal reach, which is the tension the rest of the psalm lives in.

Then a line that has been altered, and the alteration is the point. In the Psalter this verse says that he remembers his covenant forever. Here it says: Remember his covenant forever, the word that he commanded, for a thousand generations. God's faithfulness has been turned into Israel's homework.

Both are true and the second depends on the first. God does not need reminding; the covenant is safe whether or not anybody in Jerusalem thinks about it before breakfast. But the people who forget it live like people with no covenant, and Israel had just come through forty years of exactly that — nobody cancelled the ark, they simply stopped thinking about it, and a generation grew up who had never seen it.

What is to be remembered is then named, and it is a chain of three: the covenant that he made with Abraham, his sworn promise to Isaac, which he confirmed to Jacob as a statute, to Israel as an everlasting covenant. Made, sworn, confirmed. God said it to one man, swore it to his son, and fixed it as a statute on his grandson, and the promise outlived all three of them by a thousand years before this psalm was sung, and by three thousand since.

And its content is quoted: To you I will give the land of Canaan, as your portion for an inheritance. The congregation singing that line is standing on the land in question. The people who first read it in this book were living on a fraction of it under a Persian governor, singing the same words, which is a harder and better thing to do.

verseByVerse.quote: When you were few in number, of little account, and sojourners in it, wandering from nation to nation, from one kingdom to another people, he allowed no one to oppress them; he rebuked kings on their account, saying, "Touch not my anointed ones, do my prophets no harm!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the second alteration, and it is one word.

The psalm as it stands in the Psalter describes the patriarchs: when they were few in number. Here it reads: When you were few in number, of little account, and sojourners in it, wandering from nation to nation, from one kingdom to another people.

You. The line has been swung round to face the singers. And consider who was singing it when this book was compiled — a community of returned exiles, a few thousand people in a half-rebuilt town, of no political consequence to anybody, who had been moved from one empire to another twice in living memory. Few in number and of little account is not a poetic flourish to them. It is the census.

And the point is not that God pities small people. It is that the covenant which the whole psalm rests on was made with three men who had no land, no army, no standing and no descendants worth counting, and who moved between kingdoms at the mercy of whoever was hosting them. Smallness was the condition God chose to work in, and it always has been.

Then what he did about them: he allowed no one to oppress them; he rebuked kings on their account, saying, Touch not my anointed ones, do my prophets no harm!

God went into Pharaoh's palace over Sarah and into Abimelech's dreams over her, and both times a king with an army was told to keep his hands off a wandering herdsman. And listen to the titles. My anointed ones. My prophets. Abraham owned a burial cave and a well he had to argue for; God calls him an anointed one, which is the word that will one day be Messiah, and puts him under the same protection as a throne.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The second movement turns outward. Sing to the LORD, all the earth, and declare his glory among the nations (vv. 23-24), because the gods of the peoples are nothings and the LORD made the heavens (vv. 25-26). Then the summons is put to the nations directly: Ascribe to the LORD, O families of the peoples ... bring an offering and come before him (vv. 28-29). Heaven, earth, sea and field are called in (vv. 30-32), and the last line hands the song to the trees: then shall the trees of the forest sing for joy before the LORD, for he comes to judge the earth (v. 33).
verseByVerse.theology: The LORD reigns (v. 31) is sung on the day a tent was pitched on a small ridge in a minor kingdom. It is not a description of what the news looked like. It is a statement about who holds the throne, sung by people who could see very little evidence of it out of the window.
verseByVerse.examples: The trees sing because judgement is coming. That is not how the word is usually heard, and creation does not hear it the way we do: for everything that has been groaning under human misrule, a judge arriving is the best news there is.

verseByVerse.quote: Sing to the LORD, all the earth! Tell of his salvation from day to day. Declare his glory among the nations, his marvelous works among all the peoples! For great is the LORD, and greatly to be praised, and he is to be feared above all gods. For all the gods of the peoples are worthless idols, but the LORD made the heavens. Splendor and majesty are before him; strength and joy are in his place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The song turns outward here and never really turns back. Sing to the LORD, all the earth! Tell of his salvation from day to day. Declare his glory among the nations, his marvelous works among all the peoples!

Every horizon in those two verses is the whole world. The ark has just been installed in one tent in one city belonging to one tribe of one small nation, and the liturgy written for the occasion spends its central movement addressing the peoples who were not invited.

The reason is given in the next two lines, and it is a comparison. Great is the LORD, and greatly to be praised, and he is to be feared above all gods. For all the gods of the peoples are worthless idols, but the LORD made the heavens.

The word behind worthless idols is a mocking one — nothings, non-entities, a word that sounds in Hebrew like the word for gods and means the opposite. And the contrast is not that Israel's God is stronger. It is that theirs were made and ours makes. Every god in every temple on that coast had a workshop it came out of and a craftsman who could tell you what it cost. The LORD made the heavens, and there is no category in which the two things can be compared.

One clause describes what it is like where he is: Splendor and majesty are before him; strength and joy are in his place. Strength and joy, together, in the same sentence, as the atmosphere of the sanctuary. Not strength and terror. Not joy and sentiment. The place where God is, is the place where power and gladness turn out to be the same weather.

verseByVerse.quote: Ascribe to the LORD, O families of the peoples, ascribe to the LORD glory and strength! Ascribe to the LORD the glory due his name; bring an offering and come before him! Worship the LORD in the splendor of holiness; tremble before him, all the earth; yes, the world is established; it shall never be moved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the nations are addressed directly, and told to do what Israel is doing. Ascribe to the LORD, O families of the peoples, ascribe to the LORD glory and strength! Ascribe to the LORD the glory due his name.

Ascribe means hand over what belongs to him. It is not a request for compliments; it is the return of property. The glory is his already and the peoples have been assigning it elsewhere, and the psalm calls them in to give it back.

Notice what they are told to hand over: glory and strength. Strength has been running quietly through this psalm. The congregation was told to seek the LORD and his strength; the sanctuary was described as the place where strength and joy are; and now the nations are told to ascribe strength to him. Israel seeks it, God has it, and everyone else is called to admit whose it is — and at no point in the three verses is anybody encouraged to think that he has any of his own.

Then the invitation, which is the surprising part. Bring an offering and come before him!

Foreigners are being told to come into the courts of Israel's God with a gift in their hands. Not to admire from a distance, not to send tribute by messenger, but to come. On the day the ark entered Jerusalem the song appointed for it was already looking at Ammonites and Phoenicians and Egyptians and telling them there was room.

And the terms are set out in the same breath: Worship the LORD in the splendor of holiness; tremble before him, all the earth. Come, and tremble. The door is wide open and what is on the other side of it is holy, and both halves of that have to be said or neither has been.

And a clause that steadies everything: yes, the world is established; it shall never be moved. Sung by a nation that had been overrun by Philistines in living memory, and sung again, later, by people who had watched their city burn.

verseByVerse.quote: Let the heavens be glad, and let the earth rejoice, and let them say among the nations, "The LORD reigns!" Let the sea roar, and all that fills it; let the field exult, and everything in it! Then shall the trees of the forest sing for joy before the LORD, for he comes to judge the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let the heavens be glad, and let the earth rejoice, and let them say among the nations, The LORD reigns!

Two words in Hebrew, and they are the summary of the psalm and of the book. Not the LORD will reign one day, and not the LORD reigns in Israel. He reigns, present tense, over the nations who have not heard of him yet.

Weigh who is singing it. A tribal confederation with a new king, a tent instead of a temple, Philistines on the plain and Ammonites over the river and Egypt to the south, standing on a ridge that any serious empire could have taken in a fortnight. The evidence available to them for the sentence they were singing was almost nil, and it was true.

Then creation joins in, and the order it comes in matters. Let the sea roar, and all that fills it; let the field exult, and everything in it! Then shall the trees of the forest sing for joy before the LORD. Sea, field, forest — the parts of the world that have no interest in Israelite politics — are called to make a noise.

And the reason given is the one nobody expects. The trees sing for joy for he comes to judge the earth.

Judgement is the good news in that sentence. It is not how the word usually lands, because we hear it as a threat and we are right to. But consider it from the standpoint of a forest, or a river, or anything at all that has spent its existence under human management. The arrival of a judge means that at last somebody with the authority to do it is going to come and put the whole thing right. Everything that has been groaning is waiting for exactly that, and when it hears he is on the way, it applauds.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 34–36 — His Steadfast Love Endures Forever
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The psalm ends with the line Israel would sing for the rest of its history — Oh give thanks to the LORD, for he is good; for his steadfast love endures forever (v. 34) — and then a petition that does not belong to this day at all: Save us, O God of our salvation, and gather and deliver us from among the nations (v. 35). It closes in doxology, and the crowd answers: Then all the people said, Amen! and praised the LORD (v. 36).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 35 is a prayer for exiles, put into the mouth of a congregation that was not in exile and had no idea it ever would be. The people who first read this book had come back from Babylon, and they found their own prayer already written into the first psalm ever sung before the ark.
verseByVerse.examples: That refrain went everywhere afterwards. It was sung when the temple was dedicated and when fire came down on it, by a choir marching in front of an army, and by builders laying the foundation of a much smaller house with old men weeping in the crowd.

verseByVerse.quote: Oh give thanks to the LORD, for he is good; for his steadfast love endures forever! Say also: "Save us, O God of our salvation, and gather and deliver us from among the nations, that we may give thanks to your holy name and glory in your praise. Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, from everlasting to everlasting!" Then all the people said, "Amen!" and praised the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Oh give thanks to the LORD, for he is good; for his steadfast love endures forever!

This line goes on to have a career. It is sung when Solomon's temple is dedicated and the glory fills the house so that the priests cannot stand up. It is sung when fire falls on the altar. Jehoshaphat puts a choir in front of his army and sends them out to face three nations singing it. Two exiled generations later, when the foundation of a much smaller temple is laid and the old men who remembered the first one are weeping, that is what the builders sing. An entire psalm was eventually written with it as every second line, twenty-six times over.

The load-bearing word is steadfast love — covenant loyalty, the settled determination of God to keep faith with people who do not keep faith with him. And the claim made about it is duration. Not that it is warm or generous but that it does not stop, and the people who would eventually need that sentence most were the ones for whom everything else had stopped.

Which brings the psalm to its last petition, and it is a very odd thing to sing on this particular afternoon. Save us, O God of our salvation, and gather and deliver us from among the nations, that we may give thanks to your holy name and glory in your praise.

Gather us from among the nations. Nobody was scattered. The tribes had just come in from every corner of the land to Hebron and then to Jerusalem; this is the most gathered day in Israel's history to date. The prayer does not fit the occasion at all.

It fits the readers. The people holding this book had come back from Babylon, and most of their relatives had not come back, and the word gather was the word their whole generation lived on. The Chronicler has put their prayer into the first song ever sung before the ark, so that when they said it they were not adding a modern complaint to an ancient liturgy. They were singing what David appointed to be sung, and it was already about them.

Then the last line, and the crowd takes it. Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, from everlasting to everlasting! Then all the people said, Amen! and praised the LORD. The choir stops and the nation answers with one word, and the word means: let it be so, we are in this.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Then the standing arrangements, and they are strange. Asaph and his brothers are left before the ark in Jerusalem to minister daily, with Obed-edom and sixty-eight others as gatekeepers (vv. 37-38). But Zadok and the priests are left before the tabernacle of the LORD in the high place that was at Gibeon, to offer the burnt offerings morning and evening to do all that is written in the Law of the LORD (vv. 39-40), with Heman and Jeduthun and their instruments (vv. 41-42). Then everyone goes home, and David went home to bless his household (v. 43).
verseByVerse.theology: Israel's worship is now in two places. The ark has singing and no altar; the altar has sacrifice and no ark. Neither site is whole, and both are obedient, and it stays that way for a generation. Everything David does for the rest of this book is aimed at the day the two halves are one house.
verseByVerse.examples: The greatest day of public worship in Israel's history ends with the crowd dispersing to their own front doors, and the king walking to his to bless the people who live in it.

verseByVerse.quote: So David left Asaph and his brothers there before the ark of the covenant of the LORD to minister regularly before the ark as each day required, and also Obed-edom and his sixty-eight brothers, while Obed-edom, the son of Jeduthun, and Hosah were to be gatekeepers. And he left Zadok the priest and his brothers the priests before the tabernacle of the LORD in the high place that was at Gibeon to offer burnt offerings to the LORD on the altar of burnt offering regularly morning and evening, to do all that is written in the Law of the LORD that he commanded Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the standing arrangements, and they are stranger than they look.

So David left Asaph and his brothers there before the ark of the covenant of the LORD to minister regularly before the ark as each day required, with Obed-edom and sixty-eight of his brothers, and Obed-edom and Hosah on the gates. That is Jerusalem settled: the ark, a tent, a choir, doorkeepers, and daily ministry.

Count Obed-edom's people while passing. He arrived in this story three chapters ago as a man with a house on a side road, who took in an object nobody else would touch. He is here with sixty-eight brothers, on the permanent staff of the ark, and by the time the temple rosters are drawn up his family holds the gates with sixty-two more. The household that sheltered the ark for three months has become one of the clans that serve it.

And then verse 39. And he left Zadok the priest and his brothers the priests before the tabernacle of the LORD in the high place that was at Gibeon.

The tabernacle. The tent Moses made at Sinai, with the bronze altar in front of it, is still standing — six miles away, on another hill, and it has the altar. So the priests stay there to offer the burnt offering regularly morning and evening, to do all that is written in the Law of the LORD that he commanded Israel.

Read the two halves together and the problem is plain. In Jerusalem there is the ark, which is the throne and the presence, and there is no altar, so no blood can be shed there. At Gibeon there is the altar and the daily sacrifice and the full order of the law, and the ark is not there, so the mercy seat is bare and the Most Holy Place is empty. Israel's worship has been cut in two, and each half is doing exactly what it has been told, and neither half is whole.

David does not resolve it, because he cannot. He keeps both, obediently, and hands the problem forward. Everything he does in the rest of this book — the site bought on a threshing floor, the plans, the gold, the courses of priests, the charge to his son — is aimed at the day the throne and the altar stand under one roof.

They did, for a while, and then that house came down too. The presence of God and the place where blood is shed were finally brought together in one location on a hill outside Jerusalem, in a man who was himself the altar and the offering and the mercy seat and the throne, and there has been no need for a second address since.

verseByVerse.quote: With them were Heman and Jeduthun and the rest of those chosen and expressly named to give thanks to the LORD, for his steadfast love endures forever. Heman and Jeduthun had trumpets and cymbals for the music and instruments for sacred song. The sons of Jeduthun were appointed to the gate.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Heman and Jeduthun are at Gibeon too, and the rest of those chosen and expressly named to give thanks to the LORD, for his steadfast love endures forever.

Chosen and expressly named. Somebody wrote a list, and the list was of men whose duty was gratitude. It is a curious thing to be appointed to by name — not to guard a gate or kill a bull, but to say thank you, on the record, in a rota, at a sanctuary six miles from where the crowd was.

And the refrain is quoted again, one verse after it was sung, as though the Chronicler cannot let it go: for his steadfast love endures forever. It has become the standing text at both sanctuaries. The ark has it in Jerusalem and the altar has it at Gibeon, and whichever hill an Israelite climbed he heard the same sentence about God.

Jeduthun is a name worth carrying away. Three psalms still standing in the Psalter are headed to him or set to his manner, and one of them is the prayer of a man who kept his mouth shut so hard that his heart grew hot within him, and who ended by asking God to look away so that he might smile again before he went. That is on the list of men appointed to give thanks. Thanksgiving as an office does not require a man who has never been in the dark.

Then the instruments and the doors — trumpets and cymbals for the music, and the sons of Jeduthun appointed to the gate. The men who play and the men who stand at the entrance are listed in one breath, at equal length, with the same care.

verseByVerse.quote: Then all the people departed each to his house, and David went home to bless his household.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then all the people departed each to his house, and David went home to bless his household.

The crowd disperses. The greatest day of worship in the nation's history to that point ends the way every service ends — with people walking home to their own front doors, to supper, and to whatever was waiting for them there.

And the king goes to do at his own table what he has just done at the ark. He blessed the people in the name of the LORD in verse 2; now he goes home to bless his household. The same man, the same blessing, a smaller room. Whatever was true in front of three hundred thousand people had to be true in a house with his children in it, and the last thing recorded of the day is that he went to make it so.

The other account of this day does not stop here. It follows him through the door and records who was waiting for him and what she said, and it is not a happy scene. The Chronicler leaves him on the threshold, walking home to bless his family, and closes the chapter there.

It is a right place to stop. The ark is at rest, the song has been appointed, the nations have been summoned, and the last picture is a man going in to pray for the people who live with him. That is where the ark was always heading — not into a building, but into the ordinary rooms of a people God had decided to live among, and the God who came into a tent on a ridge has since come nearer than that, and does not go home at the end of the day, because he is already there.

16.theology:
Verses 10 and 11 are the centre of the book's argument, and the object of the verb has been moving. Saul did not seek the LORD and died (10:14). David set out to seek it, the ark, and a man was killed (13:3). He learned to seek him according to the rule (15:13). And here the whole congregation is told to seek his presence continually — his face — on the very day the object has been found and installed twenty yards away. Having God is not the end of seeking God.

And the psalm has been turned to face the singers. Where the Psalter says he remembers his covenant, this says remember it (v. 15); where it says they were few in number, this says you were (v. 19); and the closing petition asks God to gather us from among the nations (v. 35) on a day when nobody was scattered. The first song ever sung before the ark was written to fit people who would not be born for five hundred years.
16.examples:
Every person in the crowd went home with bread and meat in their hands, men and women, with no list and no ranking. A day of high worship ended in food handed out to everybody who turned up, and that is not a footnote to the theology of the chapter; it is the theology of the chapter with a loaf in it.

The trumpets were to sound regularly, and the singers were appointed as each day required. The hardest part of what was set up on that afternoon was not the procession but the Tuesday after it, and Scripture takes the trouble to say so.

The day closes with the king walking home to bless his own household. He had blessed a nation a few hours earlier. The blessing that costs most is usually the one given at your own table, to the people who know exactly what you are like.

17.title: The Davidic Covenant: God's Promise That Changes Everything
17.text: <sup>1</sup>Now when David lived in his house, David said to Nathan the prophet, "Behold, I dwell in a house of cedar, but the ark of the covenant of the LORD is under a tent."<sup>2</sup>And Nathan said to David, "Do all that is in your heart, for God is with you."<sup>3</sup>But that same night the word of the LORD came to Nathan,<sup>4</sup>"Go and tell my servant David, 'Thus says the LORD: It is not you who will build me a house to dwell in.<sup>5</sup>For I have not lived in a house since the day I brought up Israel to this day, but I have gone from tent to tent and from dwelling to dwelling.<sup>6</sup>In all places where I have moved with all Israel, did I speak a word with any of the judges of Israel, whom I commanded to shepherd my people, saying, "Why have you not built me a house of cedar?"'<sup>7</sup>Now, therefore, thus shall you say to my servant David, 'Thus says the LORD of hosts, I took you from the pasture, from following the sheep, to be prince over my people Israel,<sup>8</sup>and I have been with you wherever you have gone and have cut off all your enemies from before you. And I will make for you a name, like the name of the great ones of the earth.<sup>9</sup>And I will appoint a place for my people Israel and will plant them, that they may dwell in their own place and be disturbed no more. And violent men shall waste them no more, as formerly,<sup>10</sup>from the time that I appointed judges over my people Israel. And I will subdue all your enemies. Moreover, I declare to you that the LORD will build you a house.<sup>11</sup>When your days are fulfilled to walk with your fathers, I will raise up your offspring after you, one of your own sons, and I will establish his kingdom.<sup>12</sup>He shall build a house for me, and I will establish his throne forever.<sup>13</sup>I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son. I will not take my steadfast love from him, as I took it from him who was before you,<sup>14</sup>but I will confirm him in my house and in my kingdom forever, and his throne shall be established forever.'"<sup>15</sup>In accordance with all these words, and in accordance with all this vision, Nathan spoke to David.<sup>16</sup>Then King David went in and sat before the LORD and said, "Who am I, O LORD God, and what is my house, that you have brought me thus far?<sup>17</sup>And this was a small thing in your eyes, O God. You have also spoken of your servant's house for a great while to come, and have shown me future generations, O LORD God!<sup>18</sup>And what more can David say to you for honoring your servant? For you know your servant.<sup>19</sup>For your servant's sake, O LORD, and according to your own heart, you have done all this greatness, in making known all these great things.<sup>20</sup>There is none like you, O LORD, and there is no God besides you, according to all that we have heard with our ears.<sup>21</sup>And who is like your people Israel, the one nation on earth whom God went to redeem to be his people, making for yourself a name for great and awesome things, in driving out nations before your people whom you redeemed from Egypt?<sup>22</sup>And you made your people Israel to be your people forever, and you, O LORD, became their God.<sup>23</sup>And now, O LORD, let the word that you have spoken concerning your servant and concerning his house be established forever, and do as you have spoken,<sup>24</sup>and your name will be established and magnified forever, saying, 'The LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, is Israel's God,' and the house of your servant David will be established before you.<sup>25</sup>For you, my God, have revealed to your servant that you will build a house for him. Therefore your servant has found courage to pray before you.<sup>26</sup>And now, O LORD, you are God, and you have promised this good thing to your servant.<sup>27</sup>Now you have been pleased to bless the house of your servant, that it may continue forever before you, for it is you, O LORD, who have blessed, and it is blessed forever."
17.overview:
Settled in the cedar house Hiram built him, David tells Nathan he means to build the ark a house, and Nathan approves (vv. 1-2). That night God overrules the prophet: David will not build him a house, and God has never asked any leader of Israel for one (vv. 3-6). Instead God rehearses what he has done for David and turns the word round — the LORD will build you a house (vv. 7-10). A son will build the building; the dynasty will be God's own, father to son, and the steadfast love will not be withdrawn as it was from Saul (vv. 11-15). David then goes in, sits down before the LORD, and prays (vv. 16-27).

The chapter turns on one word with two meanings. David offered God a building; God gave David a family. And in this book the promise is put in a form the account in Samuel does not use — my house and my kingdom — because the throne in Jerusalem belongs to God, which is why it could outlive every man who ever sat on it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — A House of Cedar and a Tent
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David, settled at last in the cedar house Hiram's men built him, cannot enjoy it: I dwell in a house of cedar, but the ark of the covenant of the LORD is under a tent (v. 1). Nathan tells him to go ahead — Do all that is in your heart, for God is with you (v. 2) — and that same night God overrules the prophet (v. 3). The message is blunt: It is not you who will build me a house to dwell in (v. 4). And the reason is not that the plan is unworthy but that God has never asked for one. He has gone from tent to tent and from dwelling to dwelling (v. 5), and never in four hundred years said to a single judge, Why have you not built me a house of cedar? (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: God's silence about his own accommodation is the striking thing here. He moved house every time Israel moved, for centuries, and never once mentioned it. The initiative in this chapter was never going to be a man's, and the reason is that God had no unmet need for a man to meet.
verseByVerse.examples: Nathan gave sincere, godly-sounding advice on his own authority and was wrong. God corrected him the same night, before the king had laid a stone, and the prophet went back in the morning and said the opposite of what he had said the day before.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when David lived in his house, David said to Nathan the prophet, "Behold, I dwell in a house of cedar, but the ark of the covenant of the LORD is under a tent." And Nathan said to David, "Do all that is in your heart, for God is with you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The house is finished. Hiram's masons have gone home, the cedar is up, and for the first time in his life David is living somewhere that does not have to be struck and carried. He has been in caves, in a Philistine border town, in a stronghold in the wilderness and in a tent at Hebron. Now he has a roof of Lebanon cedar.

And he cannot enjoy it. Behold, I dwell in a house of cedar, but the ark of the covenant of the LORD is under a tent.

Nothing has gone wrong. The ark is exactly where he put it, in a tent he pitched for it, with a choir singing round it every day. It is not neglect that is bothering him; it is the comparison. He has become the first man in Israel whose accommodation is better than God's, and the moment he notices it he cannot leave it alone.

Comfort did that. It is not a bad instinct, and it arrived only because David finally had time to sit still and look around. A man in a cave does not compare his roof with anyone's.

Then Nathan answers, and Nathan is wrong. Do all that is in your heart, for God is with you.

It sounds unimpeachable. The heart in question is a devout one, the project is generous, and the observation that God is with David is simply true; the Chronicler has said so himself. But the prophet has not been told anything. He has read the situation, admired the impulse, and issued a verdict in the name of a God who has not spoken, and the fact that his advice was warm and pious did not make it right.

verseByVerse.quote: But that same night the word of the LORD came to Nathan, "Go and tell my servant David, 'Thus says the LORD: It is not you who will build me a house to dwell in. For I have not lived in a house since the day I brought up Israel to this day, but I have gone from tent to tent and from dwelling to dwelling. In all places where I have moved with all Israel, did I speak a word with any of the judges of Israel, whom I commanded to shepherd my people, saying, "Why have you not built me a house of cedar?"'
verseByVerse.commentary:
But that same night the word of the LORD came to Nathan.

That same night. Not a month later, after the foundations were dug and the king had announced a building programme. Before anyone had picked up a tool, God overturned the advice of his own prophet, and the speed of it is a mercy to both men.

And the message is flat. It is not you who will build me a house to dwell in. In the parallel account God asks it as a question. Here it is a statement with no room in it, and the reader is left to notice that God can say a plain no to a good man's best idea.

Then the reason, and the reason is not what anyone would guess. Not you are unworthy. Not the timing is wrong. Instead: I have not lived in a house since the day I brought up Israel to this day, but I have gone from tent to tent and from dwelling to dwelling.

Four hundred years of that. Every time Israel struck camp in the wilderness, God moved. Every time the tabernacle was taken down and carried on poles and set up in a new place — Gilgal, Shiloh, Nob, Gibeon — the God of heaven went with them and lived where they lived. He has been, by his own description, a God without a fixed address, because his people did not have one either.

Then the question that closes the argument. Did I speak a word with any of the judges of Israel, whom I commanded to shepherd my people, saying, Why have you not built me a house of cedar?

Never once. Through Deborah and Gideon and Jephthah and Samson and Eli and Samuel, through the whole disorderly stretch of the judges, God never complained about his accommodation to anybody. It had not occurred to him to want it. The God who owns the cedars of Lebanon has no housing need for a king to meet, and that is why the offer, however sincere, had the whole relationship the wrong way round.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–15 — I Will Build You a House
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God rehearses David's life in verbs that are all his own: I took you from the pasture, from following the sheep, I have been with you, I have cut off your enemies, and I will make for you a name (vv. 7-8). He promises the people a place where they will be planted and undisturbed (vv. 9-10a). Then the turn on which everything hinges: the LORD will build you a house (v. 10b). A son will build the building; God will build the dynasty (vv. 11-12). I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son — and this steadfast love will not be withdrawn as it was from Saul (v. 13). Nathan then reports it all, exactly (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: The word for house means a building and a family, and the chapter turns on the second meaning. David offered God a roof; God answered with a dynasty. And verse 14 says my house and my kingdom, where the account in Samuel says yours — the throne David sits on is God's throne, which is how this book will describe it to the end.
verseByVerse.examples: The promise had to be delivered by the man whose advice it contradicted. Nathan spoke it in accordance with all these words, and in accordance with all this vision (v. 15), including the part that made him look foolish.

verseByVerse.quote: Now, therefore, thus shall you say to my servant David, 'Thus says the LORD of hosts, I took you from the pasture, from following the sheep, to be prince over my people Israel, and I have been with you wherever you have gone and have cut off all your enemies from before you. And I will make for you a name, like the name of the great ones of the earth. And I will appoint a place for my people Israel and will plant them, that they may dwell in their own place and be disturbed no more. And violent men shall waste them no more, as formerly, from the time that I appointed judges over my people Israel. And I will subdue all your enemies. Moreover, I declare to you that the LORD will build you a house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Having refused the gift, God begins to give, and he starts with a biography written entirely in the first person.

I took you from the pasture, from following the sheep, to be prince over my people Israel, and I have been with you wherever you have gone and have cut off all your enemies from before you.

Every verb belongs to God. Took, been with, cut off. The man now sitting in a cedar house with a standing army and a united kingdom is reminded, in one sentence, that he was last seen walking behind sheep and that nothing in between was self-made. And the word for his office is not king but prince — one set over, appointed, under someone.

Then: And I will make for you a name, like the name of the great ones of the earth.

A name is what men have always tried to take for themselves. On a plain in Shinar they said, let us make a name for ourselves, and God came down and scattered them. Then he found one childless nomad and said, I will make your name great. It is the same offer here, and the direction is what makes it safe. David set out to build God a house; God turns it round and hands David a name, and neither one was requested by the other.

Before he comes to the dynasty, God speaks about the people. He will appoint a place, plant them, let them dwell undisturbed, and end the wasting by violent men that had gone on since the days of the judges. The covenant with the king is set inside a promise to the nation, and it always was: David is exalted for the sake of his people, exactly as he realised when the cedar first arrived.

And then the sentence turns over. Moreover, I declare to you that the LORD will build you a house.

verseByVerse.quote: When your days are fulfilled to walk with your fathers, I will raise up your offspring after you, one of your own sons, and I will establish his kingdom. He shall build a house for me, and I will establish his throne forever. I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son. I will not take my steadfast love from him, as I took it from him who was before you, but I will confirm him in my house and in my kingdom forever, and his throne shall be established forever.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Hebrew word for house means a building and it means a family, and the whole chapter is balanced on that hinge. David said: I will build a house for the LORD, meaning stone and cedar. God says: the LORD will build you a house, meaning sons and a throne and a line that does not stop. The king offered a building and was given a dynasty, and he had no way of asking for it because it had not entered his head.

The terms follow. When your days are fulfilled to walk with your fathers, I will raise up your offspring after you, one of your own sons, and I will establish his kingdom. David will be dead before any of it happens. The promise is made to a man who will not see it, about a boy who is at this point a name on a list in chapter 14.

He shall build a house for me, and I will establish his throne forever. So David's project is not cancelled, only reassigned. He wanted to build and is told his son will, and the rest of this book shows what he did with that answer: he spent the remainder of his life buying the site, gathering the gold, drawing the plans and organising the priests for a building he would never enter.

Then the heart of it. I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son. I will not take my steadfast love from him, as I took it from him who was before you.

Saul is in that sentence without being named. Everyone reading knew what happened to the last house God set up in Israel: it lasted one generation and ended on a hill at Gilboa with four bodies and a stripped corpse. This one will not go that way, and the reason given is a relationship rather than a performance. Father and son.

The account in Samuel adds a line at this point which Chronicles leaves out — that when the son commits iniquity, God will discipline him with the rod of men. It is not that the Chronicler denies it; his own second volume is a long record of exactly that discipline falling on Solomon's line. But he is writing for people whose kings are gone and whose city has already been burned, and what he prints is the half of the promise they needed to hear: the steadfast love does not get withdrawn.

And the last verse of the promise contains the difference this book cares about most. Samuel says: your house and your kingdom shall be made sure. Chronicles says: I will confirm him in my house and in my kingdom forever.

My. The house is God's and the kingdom is God's, and David's son is confirmed inside something that was never David's to hand on. Later in this book the throne in Jerusalem is called the throne of the kingdom of the LORD, and Solomon is said to have sat on the throne of the LORD, and it is this verse that licenses both. Israel's monarchy is a tenancy in God's own kingdom, and that is why it could survive the loss of every king who ever held it.

Centuries on, a letter written to Jewish believers asks which of the angels God ever spoke to like this, and quotes the line: I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son. The son in view is not Solomon, whose throne lasted four hundred years and then fell. It is the one whose kingdom the word forever was always waiting for.

verseByVerse.quote: In accordance with all these words, and in accordance with all this vision, Nathan spoke to David.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In accordance with all these words, and in accordance with all this vision, Nathan spoke to David.

All these words. All this vision. The verse takes the trouble to say twice that nothing was left out, and what could most easily have been left out is the beginning of it, where God says a plain no to the plan Nathan had blessed the day before.

So the prophet walked back into the throne room and told the king that yesterday's counsel had been overruled. He does not seem to have softened it, and he does not seem to have made excuses. The record simply notes that he delivered the whole thing, and then leaves him out of the rest of the chapter.

He will come back. The next time this man walks in with a word from God about David's house it will be about a lamb and a rich man and a sin nobody else dared name, and he will not soften that either.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David goes in and sat before the LORD, and what comes out is not a policy but a question: Who am I, O LORD God, and what is my house, that you have brought me thus far? (v. 16). God has spoken of his house for generations to come and shown him the future (v. 17), and David runs out of words — what more can David say to you for honoring your servant? For you know your servant (v. 18). It was done, he says, according to your own heart (v. 19). Then the prayer turns to two incomparables: there is none like you (v. 20), and who is like your people Israel, the one nation God went in person to redeem (vv. 21-22).
verseByVerse.theology: The reason given for the whole covenant is God's own heart. Not David's record, not the ark, not the cedar. God did it because of what he is like, which is the only foundation that does not move.
verseByVerse.examples: He sat down. The posture is odd enough that the writer records it, and it is the posture of a man who has just been told he is not a subject at an audience but a son in a family.

verseByVerse.quote: Then King David went in and sat before the LORD and said, "Who am I, O LORD God, and what is my house, that you have brought me thus far? And this was a small thing in your eyes, O God. You have also spoken of your servant's house for a great while to come, and have shown me future generations, O LORD God! And what more can David say to you for honoring your servant? For you know your servant. For your servant's sake, O LORD, and according to your own heart, you have done all this greatness, in making known all these great things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then King David went in and sat before the LORD.
